58102.e: When the ground shakes, the casing moves with the ground, while the heavy mass stays almost still because of its inertia. The relative movement is recorded.
58102.m: A seismograph uses the inertia of a mass.

58103.q: What is the difference between a seismometer and a seismograph?
a: The seismometer measures, the seismograph also records
There is no difference in technical language
58103.e: The seismometer is the sensor for ground movement. Together with a recording unit it makes a seismograph, which produces a seismogram.
58103.m: A seismograph measures and records ground movements.

58104.q: Why do modern seismometer stations have three measuring components?
a: To record north-south, east-west and vertical movement
To measure three different earthquakes at once
To separate P, S and surface waves
To cover day, night and weekends
58104.e: Ground movements happen in all directions. With three sensors at right angles to each other, the complete movement can be reconstructed.
58104.m: A three-component seismometer measures movements in all three directions.

58105.q: In which country did modern seismology develop especially early because of the many earthquakes in the late 19th century?
58105.e: Researchers such as the Briton John Milne built sensitive seismographs in Tokyo. Japan thus became a centre of early earthquake research.
58105.m: Japan was an early centre of earthquake research.

58107.q: What did Ernst von Rebeur-Paschwitz record for the first time in Potsdam in 1889?
58107.e: His horizontal pendulum recorded waves from an earthquake in Japan. This proved for the first time that earthquake waves travel through the whole globe.
58107.m: Since 1889 we have known that distant earthquakes can be measured worldwide.

58108.q: What does the word “seismograph” literally mean in Greek?
58108.e: It is made up of “seismos” for shaking and “graphein” for writing.

58109.q: What is special about a broadband seismometer?
a: It records very slow to fast ground vibrations
It only measures earthquakes above magnitude 8
58109.e: Broadband instruments measure vibrations with periods from fractions of a second to several hundred seconds. This means near and distant earthquakes can be analysed equally well.
58109.m: Broadband seismometers measure a very wide range of frequencies.

58110.q: Which instrument is used near the focus so that very strong ground movements do not overload it?
58110.e: Sensitive seismometers reach their limits in strong shaking. Strong-motion instruments measure ground acceleration even in severe earthquakes, for example for earthquake-proof buildings.
58110.m: Strong ground movements are measured with accelerometers.

58111.q: Apart from earthquake research, what task does a worldwide network of seismometers carry out?
58111.e: Underground nuclear explosions produce ground waves like small earthquakes. The international monitoring system for the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty therefore uses seismometers all over the world.
58111.m: Seismometers can also detect nuclear tests.

58112.q: Why does an oceanic plate sink beneath a continental plate when they collide?
a: It is thicker than the continental plate
58112.e: Oceanic lithosphere made of basalt is denser than continental crust. That is why it sinks into the Earth's mantle.
58112.m: The denser oceanic plate sinks beneath the lighter continental one.

58113.q: What are the extremely strong thrust earthquakes at the boundary of a subduction zone called?
58113.e: At the locked boundary between the plates, stress builds up over centuries. When it is released, the strongest earthquakes on Earth happen.
58113.m: The strongest earthquakes are megathrust earthquakes at subduction zones.

58114.q: What is the wedge of scraped-off sediments at the edge of the upper plate called?
58114.e: As the plate sinks, sediments are scraped off the lower plate and added to the upper plate. In this way an accretionary wedge grows.
58114.m: Scraped-off sediments form an accretionary wedge at subduction zones.

58115.q: What happens when two continental plates collide?
a: A fold mountain range is piled up
One plate sinks deep into the mantle
58115.e: Continental crust is too light to sink deep. So the plates are compressed and pile up a fold mountain range, such as the Himalayas.
58115.m: When two continents collide, a fold mountain range forms.

58116.q: What happens to rock that gets to great depth in a subduction zone?
a: It is turned into new rock by high pressure
It is ground into loose sand
58116.e: Under high pressure and high temperature, new minerals form in the rock; this is called metamorphism. Typical of subduction zones is blueschist, which forms at high pressure and fairly low temperature.
58116.m: In subduction zones, rock is transformed by high pressure.

58117.q: How was the Cascadia earthquake of 1700 on the north-west coast of America dated precisely?
a: From Japanese records of a tsunami with no earthquake felt
From the diaries of Spanish sailors
From radiocarbon dating to the exact day
From measurements by an early seismograph
58117.e: In January 1700 a tsunami was recorded in Japan without the ground shaking there. Together with dead forests on the coast of North America, the earthquake could be dated to 26 January 1700.
58117.m: A tsunami can give away a distant earthquake.

58118.q: Why do subduction earthquakes trigger tsunamis especially often?
a: The sea floor is suddenly lifted
The Earth's rotation suddenly slows down
The moon pulls more strongly after the earthquake
58118.e: The upper plate is bent over years and springs back during the earthquake. The sea floor rises and pushes away the whole column of water above it.
58118.m: A suddenly lifted sea floor sets off a tsunami.

58119.q: Which force of the sinking plate is considered an important driver of plate movement?
58119.e: The cold, dense plate sinks into the mantle and pulls the rest of the plate along behind it. This slab pull is considered one of the strongest driving forces.
58119.m: The sinking plate pulls the rest of the plate along with it.

58120.q: At what time of day did the first main earthquake in Turkey and Syria happen on 6 February 2023?
58120.e: The earthquake hit people in their sleep at 4:17 local time. Many were buried in their homes, and it was also cold winter weather.
58120.m: The earthquake of 6 February 2023 happened in the middle of the night.

58121.q: What moment magnitude did the first main earthquake in Turkey on 6 February 2023 have?
58121.e: The earthquake near Kahramanmaraş reached a magnitude of 7.8. It was one of the strongest earthquakes in Turkey since measurements began.
58121.m: The first earthquake of 6 February 2023 had a magnitude of 7.8.

58122.q: What was especially unusual about the 2023 earthquake in Turkey and Syria?
a: Around 9 hours later a second earthquake above magnitude 7 followed
It triggered an eruption of Mount Ararat
It lasted over an hour without a break
It was not measured in Europe
58122.e: In the afternoon a separate earthquake of magnitude 7.5 to 7.7 followed near Elbistan on a neighbouring fault. This greatly increased the destruction.
58122.m: On 6 February 2023 two very strong earthquakes happened on the same day.

58123.q: On which fault did the main earthquake of 2023 happen?
58123.e: The East Anatolian Fault is a left-lateral strike-slip fault. The rupture stretched over around 350 km.
58123.m: The 2023 earthquake happened on the East Anatolian Fault.

58124.q: Which plate pushes from the south against the Anatolian Plate and drives the movement on the fault?
58124.e: The Arabian Plate is moving north against Eurasia. This squeezes the Anatolian Plate out sideways to the west.
58124.m: The Arabian Plate pushes Anatolia westwards.

58125.q: How many deaths did the 2023 earthquakes in Turkey and Syria cause altogether?
58125.e: Around 59,000 to 62,000 people died, over 53,000 of them in Turkey and several thousand in Syria.
58125.m: The 2023 earthquake was one of Turkey's worst disasters.

58126.q: After which province near the epicentre is the 2023 earthquake series often named?
58126.e: The epicentre of the first earthquake was near Pazarcık in Kahramanmaraş province. That is why it is also called the Kahramanmaraş earthquake.
58126.m: The 2023 earthquake series is named after Kahramanmaraş.

58127.q: Which historic city, ancient Antioch, was badly destroyed in 2023?
58127.e: Antakya in Hatay province was devastated over a large area. Historic churches and mosques also collapsed.
58127.m: Ancient Antioch is called Antakya today.

58128.q: Which earlier rule was strongly criticised in public after the 2023 earthquake?
a: A building amnesty for unapproved buildings
A ban on building near the coast
58128.e: In 2018, owners could have unapproved buildings legalised for a fee. Critics saw this as one reason for poor earthquake safety.
58128.m: Good building rules only help if they are actually followed.

58129.q: Which Swiss organisation sent a search and rescue team to Turkey in 2023?
58129.e: Swiss Rescue sent 87 specialists with search dogs to Hatay province. It includes the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC), Redog and army rescue troops, among others.
58129.m: Swiss Rescue helps after earthquakes all over the world.

58130.q: What forms at a divergent plate boundary in the ocean?
58130.e: The plates move apart, rising magma fills the gap and hardens into new oceanic crust. In this way the sea floor keeps growing.
58130.m: New sea floor forms at divergent plate boundaries.

58131.q: Which process mainly produces the magma at mid-ocean ridges?
58131.e: Hot mantle rock rises, the pressure drops and the rock starts to melt partly without any heat being added. This is called decompression melting.
58131.m: When the pressure on hot mantle drops, it partly melts.

58132.q: Which typical form of lava develops when basaltic lava comes out on the sea floor?
58132.e: In cold seawater, the surface of the lava hardens at once, and rounded, pillow-shaped bodies form. Pillow lava is typical of the ocean floor.
58132.m: Under water, basalt lava hardens into pillow lava.

58133.q: Which observation on the sea floor supported the theory of sea-floor spreading in the 1960s?
a: Symmetrical magnetic stripes on both sides of the ridges
Rocks of the same age across the whole ocean
Thick sediments right on the ridges
Granite as the main rock of the ocean floor
58133.e: On both sides of the ridges, the rocks show mirror-image stripes of normal and reversed magnetisation. Vine, Matthews and Morley interpreted this as a record of pole reversals in newly formed crust.
58133.m: The magnetic stripes on the sea floor are mirror images on both sides of the ridge.

58134.q: How does the age of the oceanic crust change with increasing distance from the mid-ocean ridge?
58134.e: The youngest crust forms at the ridge and is then pushed away to the sides. The further away, the older the sea floor.
58134.m: The further from the ridge, the older the ocean floor.

58135.q: What are hot springs on spreading ridges that give out dark, mineral-rich water called?
58135.e: Seawater seeps into the crust, is heated strongly and dissolves metal sulphides. When it comes out, these settle out and colour the water black.
58135.m: Black smokers are hot springs on the sea floor.

58136.q: Which name is another technical term for a divergent plate boundary?
58136.e: Because new lithosphere is built there, it is called constructive. Subduction zones are destructive, transform faults are conservative.
58136.m: Divergent plate boundaries build crust and are therefore called constructive.

58137.q: Which mid-ocean ridge is one of the fastest spreading on Earth?
58137.e: At the East Pacific Rise, more than 10 centimetres of new sea floor form per year in places. The Gakkel Ridge in the Arctic Ocean, by contrast, is one of the slowest.
58137.m: The East Pacific Rise spreads especially fast.

58138.q: Which US geologist published the model of sea-floor spreading in 1962?
58138.e: Harry Hess described how magma rises at the ridges and pushes the sea floor away to the sides. The model became a building block of plate tectonics.
58138.m: Harry Hess explained how the sea floor spreads.

58139.q: Why does the oceanic plate sink when an oceanic plate collides with a continental one?
58139.e: Oceanic lithosphere made of basalt is denser than the lighter continental crust. So it sinks into the mantle, which is called subduction.
58139.m: The denser oceanic plate sinks beneath the lighter continental plate.

58140.q: Which landform develops on the sea floor where a plate is subducted?
58140.e: Where the oceanic plate bends downwards, a long, very deep trench forms. The deepest is the Mariana Trench.
58140.m: There is a deep-sea trench in front of every subduction zone.

58141.q: How are the earthquake foci at a subduction zone distributed at depth?
a: All just below the Earth's surface
Scattered at random with no pattern
58141.e: The earthquake foci follow the sinking plate at a slant down to a depth of around 700 kilometres. This zone is called the Wadati-Benioff zone.
58141.m: Earthquake foci trace the slanting path of the sinking plate.

58142.q: What forms when an oceanic plate sinks beneath another oceanic plate?
58142.e: The magma from the subduction zone rises and forms an arc-shaped chain of volcanic islands. Examples are the Marianas and the Lesser Antilles.

58143.q: What is the body of sediments called that is scraped off the sinking plate and piled up at a subduction zone?
58143.e: The top layer of sediment on the sinking plate is scraped off against the upper plate and stacked in a wedge. In this way the edge of the continent grows over time.
58143.m: Scraped-off sediments form an accretionary wedge at subduction zones.

58144.q: Why does magma form above a sinking plate?
a: Released water lowers the melting point of the mantle
The plate melts completely through friction
The pressure in the mantle drops sharply
Heat from the sun reaches deep down
58144.e: Deep down, the sinking plate releases water. This rises into the mantle wedge above and lowers the melting point of the rock there.
58144.m: Water from the sinking plate makes the mantle above it melt.

58145.q: What is the force called with which a sinking, heavy plate pulls the rest of the plate along behind it?
58145.e: The cold, dense lithosphere sinks into the mantle and drags the plate after it. Slab pull is considered the most important driving force of plate tectonics.
58145.m: Slab pull is the most important driving force of plate movement.

58146.q: Why are rocks at subduction zones transformed at high pressure but relatively low temperature?
a: The cold plate sinks quickly to great depth
There is no geothermal heat at all in subduction zones
The rocks there lie right at the surface
58146.e: The cold oceanic plate quickly gets to great depth without warming up much. This creates special rocks such as blueschist.
58146.m: At subduction zones there is high pressure at comparatively low temperature.

58147.q: Roughly how deep is the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench?
58147.e: The Challenger Deep reaches almost 11,000 metres below sea level. It is the deepest known point in the oceans.
58147.m: The deepest point of the oceans is around 11 kilometres below the sea surface.

58148.q: What happens to the Earth's crust at a transform fault?
a: It is neither created nor destroyed
It is sunk into the mantle
58148.e: The plates slide sideways past each other. That is why such boundaries are also called conservative.
58148.m: At transform faults, plates slide sideways past each other.

58149.q: Between which plates does the San Andreas Fault run?
a: Juan de Fuca and Pacific Plates
58149.e: In California, the San Andreas Fault separates the Pacific Plate from the North American Plate. It is one of the best-known transform faults on land.
58149.m: The San Andreas Fault separates the Pacific and North American Plates.

58150.q: On which plate is the city of Los Angeles?
58150.e: Los Angeles lies west of the San Andreas Fault and therefore on the Pacific Plate. It is slowly moving north-west towards San Francisco.
58150.m: Los Angeles is on the Pacific Plate.

58151.q: Which devastating earthquake of 1906 was caused by the San Andreas Fault?
58151.e: In 1906 the fault ruptured over a length of several hundred kilometres. The earthquake and fires destroyed large parts of San Francisco.
58151.m: The San Francisco earthquake of 1906 happened on the San Andreas Fault.

58152.q: Roughly how fast do the plates move against each other at the San Andreas Fault?
58152.e: The Pacific Plate moves relative to the North American Plate by around 3 to 5 cm per year, about as fast as fingernails grow. Because the plates lock together, the stress is released suddenly in earthquakes.
58152.m: At the San Andreas Fault, the plates move a few centimetres per year.

58153.q: What moves the sections of a mid-ocean ridge sideways against each other?
58153.e: Mid-ocean ridges are divided into many segments offset by transform faults. Only the part between the ridge ends is active; the extensions are called fracture zones.
58153.m: Transform faults divide the ocean ridges into sections.

58154.q: Which natural hazard is typical of transform faults?
58154.e: Because the plates lock and then suddenly let go, shallow, often strong earthquakes happen. There is usually no volcanism, because no melt forms.

58155.q: Which large transform fault runs across the north of Turkey?
58155.e: The North Anatolian Fault separates the Anatolian Plate from the Eurasian Plate. There have been repeated severe earthquakes along this fault, for example near Izmit in 1999.
58155.m: The North Anatolian Fault is a transform fault in Turkey.

58156.q: Which plates slide past each other at the transform fault through the Jordan Valley and the Dead Sea?
58156.e: Here the Arabian Plate slides north past the African Plate. The Dead Sea lies in a basin along this fault.
58156.m: The Dead Sea lies on a transform fault between Arabia and Africa.

58157.q: Which two plates does the Mid-Atlantic Ridge separate in the North Atlantic?
58157.e: In the North Atlantic, the North American and Eurasian Plates are moving away from each other. On Iceland this plate boundary even comes up on land.
58157.m: In the North Atlantic, the ridge separates North America from Eurasia.

58158.q: Which island rose out of the sea from 1963 in an eruption south of Iceland?
58158.e: Surtsey formed from 1963 to 1967 in an undersea eruption in Iceland's volcanic zone. The island is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a laboratory for how living things settle new land.
58158.m: Surtsey is a young volcanic island off Iceland.

58159.q: Which island nation lies right on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, so that you can see the plate boundary on land there?
58159.e: Iceland lies over the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and also over a hotspot. That is why the ridge rises above sea level there, and the island gets about two centimetres wider every year.
58159.m: On Iceland, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge comes up on land.

58160.q: Which cartographer discovered the central valley along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge in the 1950s?
58160.e: Marie Tharp analysed echo-sounding data with Bruce Heezen and recognised a continuous rift structure on the ridge. This was an important clue to sea-floor spreading.
58160.m: Marie Tharp discovered the central valley of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

58161.q: Which measuring method was used in the 20th century to recognise the Mid-Atlantic Ridge as a continuous mountain range on the sea floor?
58161.e: An echo sounder sends sound waves to the sea floor and measures the time until the echo comes back. Many measurements together showed a huge mountain range in the middle of the Atlantic.
58161.m: The sea floor was mapped with echo sounding.

58162.q: Where on Iceland can you dive in a fissure between the North American and Eurasian Plates?
a: Silfra fissure in Thingvellir National Park
58162.e: The Silfra fissure is filled with clear glacier water. It lies in the rift area of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, which comes up on land on Iceland.
58162.m: In the Silfra fissure you dive between two continental plates.

58163.q: What happens at a mid-ocean ridge such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?
a: Two plates move apart and new crust forms
One plate sinks beneath the other
Two plates collide and fold up mountains
Two plates slide sideways past each other
58163.e: At the ridge the plates move apart, magma rises and hardens into new sea floor. This is called a divergent plate boundary.
58163.m: New sea floor forms at mid-ocean ridges.

58164.q: Which supercontinent broke apart when the Atlantic began to open?
58164.e: Around 200 million years ago, Pangaea began to split between North America and Africa. Since then the Atlantic has been growing at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
58164.m: The Atlantic formed when Pangaea broke apart.

58165.q: Which rock makes up most of the crust that forms at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?
58165.e: Basaltic magma forms from the rising mantle material. Oceanic crust therefore consists mainly of basalt and its deep-seated equivalent, gabbro.
58165.m: Oceanic crust consists mainly of basalt.

58166.q: Into which two sub-plates is the African Plate being split at the East African Rift?
58166.e: West of the rift lies the Nubian Plate, east of it the Somali Plate. The two are slowly moving away from each other.
58166.m: At the East African Rift, the Nubian and Somali Plates are separating.

58167.q: According to many geologists, what could the East African Rift become in many millions of years?
58167.e: If the stretching continues, the crust can tear apart completely and seawater can flow in. That is also how the Red Sea formed.
58167.m: A rift valley can become a new ocean.

58168.q: Which very deep lake lies in the western branch of the East African Rift?
58168.e: Lake Tanganyika is around 1,470 metres deep, making it the second-deepest lake on Earth. Lake Victoria, by contrast, lies in a shallow basin between the two branches of the rift.
58168.m: Lake Tanganyika fills a deep rift in East Africa.

58169.q: Why are there many volcanoes along the East African Rift?
a: The crust is stretched and thinner, and magma rises
An ocean plate sinks beneath Africa there
Meteorites have punched through the crust
58169.e: As the plates drift apart, the Earth's crust gets thinner, and magma from the mantle rises. This created volcanoes such as Ol Doinyo Lengai in Tanzania, which produces a rare carbonate lava.
58169.m: Where the crust is torn apart, magma rises.

58170.q: What is the region in Ethiopia, Eritrea and Djibouti called where the East African Rift, the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden meet?
58170.e: In the Afar Triangle, three rift systems meet at a triple junction. Parts of the region lie below sea level, and it is very active volcanically.
58170.m: In the Afar Triangle, three rift systems meet.

58171.q: Which volcano in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo is known for its lava lake?
58171.e: Nyiragongo lies in the western branch of the East African Rift near the city of Goma. Its very runny lava can flow away quickly, as in the eruptions of 1977, 2002 and 2021.
58171.m: Nyiragongo in the Congo has a lava lake.

58172.q: Which famous fossil of an early human relative was discovered in the Afar region in 1974?
58172.e: Lucy is a skeleton around 3.2 million years old of the species Australopithecus afarensis. In the rift, fossils are exposed by erosion of the rift shoulders.
58172.m: Lucy was found in Ethiopia in 1974.

58173.q: Which highest mountain in Africa is a volcano whose formation is linked to the East African Rift?
58173.e: Kilimanjaro is a stratovolcano around 5,895 metres high. The Rwenzori Mountains, by contrast, are an uplifted block of crust and not a volcano.
58173.m: Kilimanjaro is a volcano in East Africa.

58174.q: On average, how fast are the plates at the East African Rift moving away from each other?
a: Not at all, they are standing still
58174.e: On average, the plates drift apart by only a few millimetres per year. But sometimes it happens suddenly: in 2005 a crack around 60 km long opened up in the Afar region within days.
58174.m: Rifts usually open slowly, but sometimes suddenly.

58175.q: Roughly how many years ago did the Indian Plate begin to collide with Eurasia?
58175.e: The collision began in the Eocene around 50 million years ago. Since then India has been pushing north and lifting the Himalayas and Tibet.
58175.m: India has been pushing against Eurasia for around 50 million years.

58176.q: Which ocean closed as the Indian Plate moved north?
58176.e: In front of India lay the Tethys Ocean, whose floor sank beneath Eurasia. With the collision, this ocean between India and Asia disappeared.
58176.m: The Tethys disappeared between India and Asia.

58177.q: Which rocks form the summit of Mount Everest?
58177.e: The summit consists of limestone of the Qomolangma Formation, which was once deposited on the sea floor. The collision lifted it to almost 8,850 metres.
58177.m: The summit of Mount Everest was once sea floor.

58178.q: Why are there hardly any active volcanoes in the High Himalayas?
a: Two continental plates collide without deep subduction
The Himalayas lie on a hotspot
The crust there is especially thin
58178.e: Continental crust is too light to sink deep into the mantle. So hardly any magma forms, and instead the crust is stacked up and thickened.
58178.m: A continent-continent collision produces hardly any volcanoes.

58179.q: Roughly how thick is the Earth's crust beneath the Tibetan Plateau?
58179.e: The collision compressed and stacked up the crust. There it is about twice as thick as normal continental crust of around 35 kilometres.
58179.m: Beneath Tibet the Earth's crust is about twice as thick as normal.

58180.q: From which land mass did India finally separate around 90 million years ago?
58180.e: India first broke away from Africa together with Madagascar and separated from Madagascar in the Cretaceous. After that it moved quickly north.
58180.m: India separated from Madagascar in the Cretaceous.

58181.q: Which huge basalt layers formed around 66 million years ago when India moved over a hotspot?
58181.e: Enormous amounts of lava poured out above today's Réunion hotspot and formed the Deccan Traps. They cover large parts of western India.
58181.m: The Deccan Traps formed when India passed over a hotspot.

58182.q: Roughly how fast did India move north before the collision?
58182.e: Before the collision, India was one of the fastest plates known. After the collision it slowed to around 4 to 5 centimetres per year.
58182.m: Before the collision, India was an especially fast plate.

58183.q: Which severe earthquake of 2015 was a result of the collision of the Indian and Eurasian Plates?
58183.e: On 25 April 2015, an earthquake of magnitude 7.8 shook Nepal. It happened at the thrust fault where India is pushed beneath the Himalayas.
58183.m: The 2015 earthquake in Nepal happened at the Indian-Eurasian plate boundary.

a: By rock layers being squeezed together
By the crust being pulled apart
By erosion of a high plateau
58184.e: At convergent plate boundaries, rock layers are pushed together and bent. This creates folds, thrusts and high mountains.
58184.m: Fold mountains form when rock layers are squeezed together.

58185.q: What is the upward-arched part of a rock fold called?
58185.e: The arched-up part is called an anticline, the dipped part a syncline. Horst and graben, by contrast, belong to fault blocks.
58185.m: An anticline is the arched-up part of a fold.

58186.e: The African Plate, with a part jutting out northwards, moved against Eurasia. The ocean in between closed and the Alps were piled up.
58186.m: The Alps formed when Africa collided with Europe.

58187.q: Which Swiss World Heritage Site shows how older rocks were pushed over younger ones?
58187.e: At the Glarus Thrust, Verrucano around 250 to 300 million years old lies on top of much younger flysch. The Tectonic Arena Sardona has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2008.
58187.m: In the Tectonic Arena Sardona, old rocks lie on top of younger ones.

58188.q: What are the large, far-travelled packages of rock that shape the structure of the Alps called?
58188.e: During mountain building, whole packages of rock were sheared off and pushed over each other for long distances. These nappes often lie on younger rocks.
58188.m: The Alps are built of nappes pushed on top of each other.

58189.q: Which plate does the rock at the summit of the Matterhorn belong to?
58189.e: The Dent Blanche nappe, which the summit is made of, comes from the Adriatic promontory of the African Plate. That is why people say the Matterhorn has an African summit.
58189.m: The summit of the Matterhorn comes from the Adriatic Plate.

58190.q: Which Swiss mountain range is a young fold mountain range that gave its name to a period of Earth's history?
58190.e: The Jurassic period is named after the Jura Mountains, where its limestones are widespread. The Folded Jura was only folded in the late Miocene and the Pliocene, about 10 to 2 million years ago.
58190.m: The Jurassic period is named after the Jura Mountains.

58191.q: On which rock layer did the sedimentary cover slide off when the Folded Jura was folded?
58191.e: The soft evaporites of the Triassic acted like a lubricant. Above them, the layers were sheared off and folded by the push from the Alps.
58191.m: The Folded Jura slid off on soft salt and gypsum layers.

58192.q: Which mountain range is an old, heavily eroded fold mountain range from the Palaeozoic?
58192.e: The Urals formed in the late Palaeozoic through a continental collision. Since then they have been heavily eroded and are comparatively low today.
58192.m: The Urals are an old fold mountain range.

58193.q: Why are rocks that were once ocean floor found high up in the Alps, for example near Zermatt?
a: An ocean was closed and pushed up during mountain building
The sea reached into the Alps during the ice age
Volcanoes threw sea floor up high
Rivers carried the rock from the coast
58193.e: There was once an ocean between Africa and Europe. During the collision, pieces of its floor were pushed onto the continent and piled up with the Alps. Such remnants are called ophiolites.
58193.m: Remnants of ocean floor in the Alps show that an ocean once lay there.

58194.q: How does a fault-block mountain range form?
a: Blocks of crust are lifted or tilted along faults
58194.e: The crust breaks along faults into separate blocks. These are lifted, lowered or tilted.
58194.m: Fault-block mountains consist of uplifted blocks of crust.

58195.q: What is a block of crust lifted between faults called?
58195.e: A horst lies higher than its surroundings, a graben lower. Both typically form when the crust is stretched.
58195.m: A horst is an uplifted block.

58196.q: Which two upland ranges form the shoulders of the Upper Rhine Graben?
58196.e: As the graben sank, its edges were lifted. To the east lies the Black Forest, to the west the Vosges.
58196.m: The Black Forest and the Vosges are the edges of the Upper Rhine Graben.

58197.q: Which historical earthquake in Switzerland is linked to the southern end of the Upper Rhine Graben?
58197.e: Basel lies at the southern end of the Upper Rhine Graben, where the crust is still active. The 1356 earthquake is considered the strongest historically documented earthquake north of the Alps.
58197.m: The Basel earthquake of 1356 happened on the edge of the Upper Rhine Graben.

58198.q: What is a block lifted on one side and tilted, like the Harz, called?
58198.e: A tilted fault block (Pultscholle) is strongly lifted on one side and slopes gently down to the other, like a writing desk. The Harz and the Ore Mountains are examples.
58198.m: A tilted fault block is a block of crust set at a slant.

58199.q: Which old mountain range do the basement rocks of the Black Forest come from?
58199.e: The basement of the Black Forest is a remnant of the Variscan mountains, which formed in the Carboniferous. It was worn down and later lifted again as a fault block.
58199.m: The Black Forest is an uplifted remnant of the Variscan mountains.

58200.q: Which region in the west of the USA consists of many parallel horsts and grabens?
58200.e: In Nevada and Utah the crust is being stretched and breaks into many blocks. Uplifted horsts form mountain ranges, lowered grabens form basins.
58200.m: In the Basin and Range region, horsts and grabens alternate.

58201.q: Which type of fault typically forms on the edges of a graben when the crust is stretched?
58201.e: When the crust is stretched, the hanging-wall block slides down along a sloping surface. Reverse faults and thrust faults, by contrast, form when the crust is compressed.

58202.q: Which mountain range in California is an example of a tilted fault block?
58202.e: The Sierra Nevada is steeply lifted on its eastern side and slopes gently to the west. The Cascade Range, by contrast, is a chain of volcanoes.
58202.m: The Sierra Nevada is a tilted fault block.

58203.q: What does the term isostasy describe?
a: The floating balance of the crust on the mantle
The Earth spinning on its axis
The wandering of the magnetic poles
58203.e: The lighter crust floats on the denser mantle, which can be deformed plastically. It sinks in until there is a balance, like an iceberg in water.
58203.m: The Earth's crust floats in balance on the mantle.

58204.q: Why are the ocean floors lower than the continents?
a: Oceanic crust is denser and thinner
Seawater pushes the crust far down
There is no mantle beneath the oceans
The continents all lie on hotspots
58204.e: Oceanic crust made of basalt is heavier and thinner than continental crust made of granite. According to isostasy, it therefore floats lower in the mantle. The term isostasy was coined in 1889 by the US geologist Clarence Dutton.
58204.m: Dense, thin crust floats lower in the mantle.

58205.q: Why does the Earth's crust reach especially deep into the mantle beneath high mountains such as the Alps?
a: As with an iceberg, a tall part above needs a deep part below
The weight of the snow pushes it down
The mantle is especially hard beneath mountains
Mountains form above holes in the mantle
58205.e: According to Airy's model, the crust has a similar density everywhere but varies in thickness. For a high mountain range to float in balance, it needs a deep mountain root.

58206.q: Two blocks of crust of the same thickness float on the mantle. Which one sticks up higher?
a: The block with the lower density
The block with the higher density
The block closer to the pole
58206.e: A lighter block sinks in less deeply and therefore sticks up higher. This idea is behind Pratt's model of isostasy: higher blocks of crust are made of lighter rock.
58206.m: Lighter blocks of crust stand higher.

58207.q: According to isostasy, what share of a block of crust with a density of 2.7 g/cm³ lies below the surface of a mantle with a density of 3.3 g/cm³?
58207.e: As with an iceberg: the share below the surface equals the density of the block divided by the density of the mantle. 2.7 divided by 3.3 gives around 0.82, so around 82 per cent.
58207.m: A floating block sinks in according to the ratio of its density to the density beneath it.

58208.q: A mountain range is 5 km high. According to isostasy, roughly how deep does its mountain root reach into the mantle?
a: Several times deeper, about 20 to 25 km
58208.e: Because the crust is only a little lighter than the mantle, a mountain range needs a deep root. With 2.7 g/cm³ for the crust and 3.3 g/cm³ for the mantle, this gives 5 times 2.7 divided by 0.6, so around 22.5 km.
58208.m: A mountain root is many times deeper than the mountains are high.

58209.q: Why is Scandinavia still rising today?
a: The weight of the ice age ice sheet has gone
There is a hotspot beneath Scandinavia
58209.e: The massive ice sheet of the last ice age pushed the crust down. Since it melted, the land has been slowly rising again, by up to around 1 cm a year at the Gulf of Bothnia.
58209.m: Scandinavia is rising because the weight of the ice has gone.

58210.q: How can you see the post-glacial uplift of the land on the Swedish coast?
a: Old shorelines now lie far above the sea
Old harbours now lie under water
The coast is full of young volcanoes
The Baltic Sea gets saltier every year
58210.e: Since the ice sheet melted, the land has been rising. At the High Coast (Höga Kusten), the highest former shoreline lies around 286 metres above today's sea. The region is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
58210.m: At the High Coast, the land has risen especially strongly since the ice age.

58211.q: Roughly how much are parts of the Swiss Alps rising each year today?
58211.e: National surveys show uplift of about 1 to 1.5 millimetres a year. Part of this is an isostatic response to erosion and the melting of the glaciers.
58211.m: The Alps are rising by about a millimetre a year today.

58212.q: According to isostasy, what happens when a mountain range is worn away by erosion?
58212.e: Losing material makes the block of crust lighter. It therefore rises in the mantle, so that rocks from deep down reach the surface.
58212.m: When a mountain range is worn away, it rises again isostatically.

58213.q: When did the supercontinent Pangaea mainly exist?
58213.e: Pangaea formed towards the end of the Carboniferous and existed in the Permian and Triassic. After that it gradually broke up into smaller continents.
58213.m: Pangaea existed mainly in the Permian and Triassic.

58214.q: Which name is used for a possible future supercontinent?
58214.e: Models predict that the continents could join up again in a few hundred million years. One proposed name is Amasia, because America and Asia would merge.
58214.m: Amasia is a possible supercontinent of the distant future.

58215.q: The fossil of which freshwater reptile is found in both South America and southern Africa?
58215.e: The small Mesosaurus could not swim across the Atlantic. Its fossils on both continents show that they were once joined.
58215.m: Mesosaurus fossils prove that Africa and South America were once joined.

58216.q: Which observation first gave Wegener the idea of continental drift?
a: The matching coastlines of Africa and South America
The depth of the Mariana Trench
The position of the volcanoes on Iceland
58216.e: The coasts of West Africa and eastern South America fit together like jigsaw pieces. Wegener saw this as a sign that they had once been connected.
58216.m: The coasts of Africa and South America fit together like jigsaw pieces.

58217.q: What climate mainly prevailed in the interior of Pangaea, far from the sea?
58217.e: Moist sea air hardly reached the huge interior. That is why wide deserts were common there, as the red sandstones from the Permian and Triassic show.
58217.m: The interior of Pangaea was very dry.

58218.q: Why was Wegener's continental drift rejected for a long time?
a: He could not explain a driving mechanism
He disputed the age of the Earth
He did not know the continents precisely
58218.e: Wegener could not convincingly explain which force moves the continents. Only plate tectonics in the 1960s provided a mechanism.
58218.m: At first, Wegener's theory lacked a driving mechanism.

58219.q: Which present-day continent was not part of Gondwana?
58219.e: Gondwana included South America, Africa, Antarctica, Australia, India, Madagascar and Arabia. North America belonged to Laurasia.
58219.m: North America was not part of Gondwana.

58220.q: Where does the name Gondwana come from?
58220.e: The name comes from Sanskrit and means “forest of the Gond”, a people in central India. The Austrian geologist Eduard Suess adopted it in 1885 for the southern continent.
58220.m: Gondwana is named after a region in India.

58221.q: Which fossil plant occurs on all the Gondwana continents and proves they were once connected?
58221.e: Glossopteris was a seed fern whose seeds could not be spread across oceans. Its fossils are found in South America, Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica.
58221.m: Glossopteris fossils link the southern continents.

58222.q: Which traces prove a great glaciation of Gondwana in the Carboniferous and Permian?
a: Glacial deposits in countries that are warm today
58222.e: In South Africa, India, South America and Australia, tillites and glacial scratches from this time are found. They only fit together if the continents were joined at the South Pole.
58222.m: Ice age traces in countries that are warm today show where Gondwana once lay.

58223.q: Which Triassic reptile was also found in Antarctica in 1969 and supported the Gondwana theory?
58223.e: Lystrosaurus was a plant-eating land animal that is also known from Africa and India. It could not cross oceans.
58223.m: Lystrosaurus lived on several parts of Gondwana.

58224.q: Which deposits of raw materials in Antarctica show that forests once grew there?
58224.e: Coal seams from the Permian are found in the Transantarctic Mountains. At that time Gondwana lay in a climate that allowed plants to grow.
58224.m: Coal in Antarctica shows that plants once grew there.

58225.q: Roughly how many years ago was Gondwana fully assembled?
58225.e: Gondwana formed towards the end of the Precambrian through the Pan-African mountain building. Later it became part of Pangaea.
58225.m: Gondwana formed at the end of the Precambrian.

58226.q: Which ocean formed between Africa and South America when Gondwana broke up?
58226.e: In the Cretaceous, South America and Africa separated. The South Atlantic opened between them.
58226.m: The South Atlantic formed between Africa and South America.

58227.q: What was the result of Antarctica separating completely from Australia and South America?
a: An ocean current circled the continent and helped it ice over
Sea level fell by several kilometres
58227.e: With the opening of the Tasmanian Gateway and the Drake Passage, the Antarctic Circumpolar Current formed. It kept warm water away and helped the ice sheet to form.
58227.m: The Circumpolar Current helped Antarctica to ice over.

58228.q: What distinguishes physical weathering from chemical weathering?
a: Rock breaks up without the minerals changing
Minerals are turned into clay minerals
58228.e: In physical (mechanical) weathering, rock is only broken into smaller pieces. Its chemical composition stays the same.
58228.m: Physical weathering breaks up rock without changing its minerals chemically.

58229.q: What is the physical weathering called that is caused by large daily temperature changes in the rock?
58229.e: During the day the rock surface heats up strongly, and at night it cools down. Repeated expansion and contraction creates stresses that make the rock crumbly.
58229.m: Insolation weathering is caused by repeated heating and cooling.

58230.q: In which climate is insolation weathering especially effective?
a: In deserts with large differences between day and night
In a permanently frozen ice sheet
58230.e: In deserts there are no clouds or plants, so the temperature differences between day and night are very large. This encourages stresses in the rock.
58230.m: Deserts with hot days and cold nights encourage insolation weathering.

58231.q: What is the shell-like flaking off of rock layers, often after pressure release, called?
58231.e: When the rock on top is worn away, the rock below expands. Shells come off parallel to the surface.
58231.m: In exfoliation, shells of rock peel off like onion skins.

58232.q: What is the weathering called in which growing plant roots widen cracks in rock?
58232.e: Roots grow into cracks and press outwards as they get thicker. This counts as physical-biological weathering.
58232.m: Root wedging shows that plants can also split rocks.

58233.q: Why does physical weathering encourage chemical weathering?
a: It increases the surface that can be attacked
It increases the lime content of the rock
It lowers the temperature in the rock
It removes water from the rock
58233.e: Broken-up rock has a much larger surface area. Water and dissolved substances can therefore attack it chemically in more places.
58233.m: The smaller the pieces of rock, the more surface chemical weathering can attack.

58234.q: Which loose weathering debris typically forms from granite when it breaks up into separate grains?
58234.e: Through weathering, granite often breaks down into a coarse-grained mixture of quartz, feldspar and mica. This material is called grus.
58234.m: Broken-down granite forms a grainy debris called grus.

58235.q: Under which climatic conditions does chemical weathering happen fastest?
58235.e: Chemical reactions need water and run faster at higher temperatures. That is why chemical weathering is strongest in the wet tropics.
58235.m: Warmth and moisture speed up chemical weathering.

58236.q: Which rule states that the speed of chemical reactions roughly doubles or triples for a temperature rise of 10 °C?
58236.e: The rule linking reaction speed and temperature (van 't Hoff rule, in German RGT rule) explains why rock weathers chemically much faster in the tropics than in cold regions.
58236.m: According to the van 't Hoff rule, reactions run much faster in warmth.

58237.q: What is the chemical weathering called in which feldspar is turned into clay minerals by water?
58237.e: In hydrolysis, silicate minerals such as feldspar react with water. Ions such as potassium are dissolved out, and clay minerals form.

58238.q: Which clay mineral forms especially often from intense chemical weathering of feldspar in the tropics?
58238.e: Kaolinite is a two-layer clay mineral and a typical end product of strong silicate weathering. It is also the main ingredient of china clay.
58238.m: Kaolinite is a typical clay mineral from heavily weathered feldspar.

58239.q: What causes the red colour of many tropical soils and desert rocks?
58239.e: Iron from minerals reacts with oxygen to form iron oxides such as haematite. These colour soils and rocks red to rusty brown.
58239.m: Oxidised iron colours soils and rocks red.

58240.q: Which acid is at work in the carbonation weathering of limestone?
a: Carbonic acid from water and CO₂
58240.e: Rainwater takes up carbon dioxide from the air and soil and forms carbonic acid. This dissolves calcium carbonate into dissolved calcium hydrogen carbonate.
58240.m: Carbonic acid from water and carbon dioxide dissolves limestone.

58241.q: Which rock dissolves fastest by solution weathering in water alone?
58241.e: Rock salt (halite) dissolves quickly even in pure water. Silicate rocks such as granite, basalt or quartzite, by contrast, are very hard to dissolve.
58241.m: Rock salt dissolves especially easily in water.

58242.q: What is the change of anhydrite into gypsum by taking in water called?
58242.e: In hydration, water is built into the crystal lattice. Anhydrite turns into gypsum and grows in volume, which can damage rock and tunnels.
58242.m: Hydration builds water into the crystal lattice and increases the volume.

58243.q: Which form of weathering does especially strong damage to marble statues and sandstone façades in cities?
58243.e: Sulphur and nitrogen oxides from exhaust fumes form acids with rainwater. These attack limy stones such as marble or sandstone bound with lime.
58243.m: Acid rain dissolves limy building stones on monuments.

58244.q: Why is the layer of weathered rock in the wet tropics often many metres thick?
a: Intense chemical weathering over a long time
58244.e: High temperatures, lots of rain and often very long undisturbed development break the rock down deeply. This creates thick weathering layers.
58244.m: In the wet tropics, chemical weathering reaches especially deep.

58245.q: By roughly what percentage does the volume of water increase when it freezes?
58245.e: Ice has a lower density than liquid water. When it freezes it expands by around 9 per cent and can widen cracks.
58245.m: Freezing water expands by around nine per cent.

58246.q: When is frost wedging most effective?
a: When frost and thaw alternate often
In heat without rain or snow
58246.e: What matters is many freeze-thaw cycles: water gets into cracks during the thaw and forces them further open when it freezes. Constant frost alone has a much weaker effect.
58246.m: Many freeze-thaw cycles make frost wedging especially effective.

58247.q: In which altitude zone of the Alps is frost wedging especially strong?
a: On the valley floor of the Central Plateau
58247.e: Above the forest line there are frequent freeze-thaw cycles and hardly any protective plant cover. That is why a lot of rock debris and scree slopes form there.
58247.m: Above the forest line, frost splits especially large amounts of rock.

58248.q: Which landform at the foot of rock faces is mainly created by frost wedging?
58248.e: Pieces of rock broken off fall down the rock face and collect at the foot of the slope. This forms cone-shaped or band-shaped scree slopes.
58248.m: Frost-split stones collect at the foot of the rock face in scree slopes.

58249.q: In which season do rockfalls caused by frost wedging happen more often in the Alps?
a: In spring when the snow melts
In high summer in dry weather
In winter under a thick blanket of snow
58249.e: In spring, frost and thaw often alternate. The ice in the cracks melts and releases loosened stones.
58249.m: In spring, the thawing ice often causes rockfalls.

58250.q: Which damage to roads happens on the same principle as frost wedging?
58250.e: Water gets into cracks in the road surface, freezes and expands. After several freeze-thaw cycles, the surface breaks up.
58250.m: Frost splits not only rocks but also road surfaces.

58251.q: Which rock is especially prone to frost wedging?
a: Rock under water in a lake
58251.e: Water must be able to get into pores and joints to exert pressure when it freezes. Jointed and porous rock takes up a lot of water.
58251.m: Where water gets into joints, frost can split the rock.

58252.q: Apart from high mountains, which climate zone is typical of strong frost wedging?
58252.e: In the tundra there are many freeze-thaw cycles and hardly any protective vegetation. Frost wedging and frost debris shape the landscape there.
58252.m: In the tundra, frost wedging shapes the landscape.

58253.q: What splits the rock in salt wedging?
a: The pressure of growing salt crystals
58253.e: Salty water gets into pores and evaporates. The growing crystals create crystallisation pressure, which loosens the rock.
58253.m: Growing salt crystals split rock from the inside.

58254.q: In which areas is salt wedging especially common?
a: In dry regions and on sea coasts
58254.e: Salt wedging needs dissolved salts and strong evaporation. Both are found in deserts and on coasts with salt spray.
58254.m: Salt wedging is especially common in deserts and on coasts.

58255.q: Which honeycomb-like hollows in rock faces often form through salt weathering?
58255.e: Tafoni are holes and niches in rocks, often arranged like honeycombs. They form mainly through salt weathering, often on coasts and in dry regions.
58255.m: Tafoni are honeycomb-like holes mostly made by salt.

58256.q: Which problem does road salt cause on buildings and bridge piers?
58256.e: Salt solution soaks into concrete and masonry. As it dries, the salt crystallises and makes surfaces flake off.
58256.m: Road salt can damage concrete and masonry through crystallisation.

58257.q: What is the weathering called in which minerals take water into their crystal lattice and so increase their volume?
58257.e: Certain minerals, for example some salts, build water molecules into their crystal lattice and expand. The resulting pressure can loosen rock; it should be clearly distinguished from hydrolysis.
58257.m: In hydration weathering, the volume grows because of water taken in.

58258.q: What are the white salt crusts that appear on damp walls called?
58258.e: Water carries dissolved salts to the surface, where it evaporates. White salt efflorescence is left behind, which can damage the masonry.
58258.m: Salt efflorescence shows that salts are crystallising in the masonry.

58259.q: Why is salt wedging in deserts often strengthened by insolation weathering?
a: The heating encourages evaporation and crystal growth
The heat turns salt into acid
The heat partly melts the rock
The cold of the night dissolves the salt
58259.e: Strong sunshine makes the water evaporate quickly, so salts crystallise. Temperature stresses also loosen the rock.
58259.m: In the desert, heat and salt crystals work on the rock together.

58260.q: Which landscape is the term karst named after?
a: A limestone plateau in Slovenia and Italy
58260.e: The name comes from the Karst (Slovenian Kras), a limestone plateau behind Trieste. Karst landforms were described scientifically there early on.
58260.m: The Karst behind Trieste gave its name to all karst landscapes.

58261.q: What are the channels formed by solution on bare limestone surfaces called, often known in Switzerland as Schratten?
58261.e: Rainwater dissolves limestone at the surface and forms sharp-edged channels and ridges. Fields of karren like this can be found, for example, on the Schrattenfluh in the Entlebuch.
58261.m: Karren or Schratten are solution channels on limestone rock.

58262.q: What do you call a place where a river in karst suddenly disappears underground?
58262.e: A ponor or swallow hole carries surface water into underground cavities. The water often comes out again far away at a karst spring.
58262.m: In a ponor, a river sinks into the karst underground.

58263.q: Where does the water that seeps underground at Lac de Joux come back to the surface?
a: At the source of the Orbe near Vallorbe
At the Rhine Falls near Schaffhausen
At the source of the Aare on the Grimsel
58263.e: The water of Lac de Joux and Lac Brenet seeps into the limestone of the Jura. It comes out again near Vallorbe as the source of the Orbe.
58263.m: The Orbe rises near Vallorbe from karst water from Lac de Joux.

58264.q: Why is karst groundwater particularly vulnerable to pollution?
a: It flows quickly and is hardly filtered
It naturally contains a lot of salt
It is always warm and encourages bacteria
It stands completely still in the rock
58264.e: In karst areas, water flows quickly through open cracks and caves to the spring. Pollutants are hardly held back or broken down on the way.
58264.m: In karst, pollutants reach spring water quickly and unfiltered.

a: A dry valley in the desert
58265.e: Dolines are rounded, bowl-shaped or funnel-shaped hollows in soluble rock. They form through solution or through the collapse of underground cavities.
58265.m: A doline is a funnel-shaped hollow in karst areas.

58266.q: Which two main types of doline are distinguished by how they formed?
58266.e: Solution dolines form when limestone is dissolved from above. Collapse dolines form when the roof of a cave falls in.
58266.m: Dolines form through solution from above or collapse from below.

58267.q: What are the water-filled collapse dolines on the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico called?
58267.e: Cenotes are karst holes that reach down to the groundwater. For the Maya they were important sources of water and sacred places.
58267.m: Cenotes are water-filled collapse dolines in Yucatán.

58268.q: Why do dolines form mainly in limestone areas?
a: Limestone is dissolved by water containing carbonic acid
Limestone is worn away by the wind
58268.e: Rainwater takes up carbon dioxide and forms weak carbonic acid. This dissolves the limestone and creates cavities that appear as hollows or collapse.
58268.m: Water containing carbonic acid dissolves limestone and shapes dolines.

58269.q: Which language does the word doline come from?
58269.e: Doline comes from the Slovenian word “dolina”, which means valley. Many karst terms come from the Dinaric Karst.
58269.m: The word doline comes from Slovenian and means valley.

58270.q: What is a dripstone that hangs down from the ceiling of a cave called?
58270.e: Stalactites grow downwards from the ceiling. Stalagmites grow upwards from the floor, and when the two join, a column forms.
58270.m: Stalactites hang from the ceiling, stalagmites stand on the floor.

58271.q: Why is limestone deposited from dripping water in caves?
a: The water releases CO₂ into the cave air
The water freezes in the cave
The cave air contains a lot of salt
The water becomes more acidic in the cave
58271.e: Seepage water contains a lot of dissolved CO₂ from the soil. In the cave, CO₂ escapes, the balance shifts and calcium carbonate is deposited.
58271.m: When CO₂ escapes from dripping water, limestone is deposited as dripstone.

58272.q: What is the limestone that dripstones are made of called?
58272.e: Dripstones consist of calcium carbonate deposited from water. This deposit is called calcareous sinter or simply sinter.
58272.m: Dripstones are made of calcareous sinter.

58273.q: Roughly how long is the Hölloch cave system in the Muota valley (canton of Schwyz) (as of 2022)?
58273.e: As of 2022, the Hölloch is about 210 kilometres long. It is considered the second longest known cave system in Europe.
58273.m: The Hölloch in the Muota valley is over 200 kilometres long.

58274.q: What are thin, hollow dripstones that hang from the ceiling like drinking straws called?
58274.e: In soda straws, the drop runs down inside a thin tube of limestone and deposits limestone at the rim. Because of their shape they are also called macaroni.
58274.m: Soda straws are hollow, thin dripstones like drinking straws.

58275.q: How fast do dripstones typically grow?
a: Usually only fractions of a millimetre per year
58275.e: The growth rate depends on the amount of water, CO₂ and temperature. It is often less than one millimetre per year, which is why large dripstones are often thousands of years old.
58275.m: Dripstones grow very slowly and are often thousands of years old.

58276.q: Why are dripstones valuable for climate research?
a: Their layers store clues about past climates
They show the direction of the Earth’s magnetic field
58276.e: Dripstones grow in layers. Isotopes and trace elements in these layers allow conclusions about the temperature and rainfall of earlier times.
58276.m: Dripstones are climate archives covering many thousands of years.

58277.q: Which cave on Lake Thun is a well-known show cave with dripstones?
58277.e: The St Beatus Caves lie above Lake Thun near Sundlauenen. They are named after Saint Beatus and are open to visitors as a show cave.
58277.m: The St Beatus Caves on Lake Thun are a well-known Swiss dripstone cave.

58278.q: What shape is a barchan dune?
58278.e: A barchan is a crescent-shaped or half-moon-shaped dune. Its two tips are called horns.
58278.m: A barchan is a crescent-shaped dune.

58279.q: In which direction do the horns of a barchan point?
58279.e: At the low edges the sand moves faster than in the higher centre. That is why the horns race ahead and point in the direction the wind is blowing.
58279.m: The horns of a barchan point downwind.

58280.q: How do the windward and leeward sides of a barchan differ?
58280.e: On the gentle windward side, the wind drives the sand upwards. On the leeward side it slides down and forms a steep slip face.
58280.m: A barchan has a gentle windward side and a steep leeward side.

58281.q: Roughly how steep is the slip face on the leeward side of a dune?
58281.e: Dry sand slides down as soon as the slope is steeper than its natural angle of repose. This is around 30 to 35 degrees.
58281.m: The lee slope of a dune is as steep as the angle of repose of dry sand.

58282.q: Under which conditions do barchans most often form?
a: Wind from one direction and little sand
Changing winds and lots of sand
Wind from one direction and a great deal of sand
Almost no wind and damp sand
58282.e: Barchans form on firm ground with a limited supply of sand and a steady wind direction. With lots of sand, transverse dunes tend to form; with changing winds, star dunes.
58282.m: Barchans need a steady wind and little sand.

58283.q: Why do small barchans move faster than large ones?
a: They consist of less sand that has to be moved
They are heavier and roll faster
They are always sheltered from the wind
58283.e: A dune moves when sand is carried from the windward side to the leeward side. In small dunes, less sand has to be moved for this.
58283.m: The smaller a barchan is, the faster it moves.

58284.q: How do grains of sand mainly move when dunes form?
58284.e: Most grains of sand are briefly lifted by the wind and bounce over the ground in flat arcs. This saltation usually happens only a few tens of centimetres above the ground.
58284.m: In saltation, sand grains bounce over the ground in flat arcs.

58285.q: Which language does the word wadi come from?
58285.e: Wadi is the Arabic word for valley or riverbed. It is part of many place names in North Africa and Arabia.
58285.m: The word wadi comes from Arabic.

58286.q: What do you call the flow of a wadi that only happens after irregular heavy rain?
58286.e: Episodic streams carry water only occasionally and irregularly. Periodic rivers, on the other hand, carry water every year at a particular season.

58287.q: Why are many wadis larger than today’s rainfall can explain?
a: Some of them formed in wetter climate phases
They were dug out by people
They were blown out by the wind
58287.e: In wetter times in the past, parts of the Sahara were green and crossed by rivers. Many wadis are therefore relics of an earlier climate.
58287.m: Many wadis date from wetter climate phases in the past.

58288.q: Which desert valley in Jordan has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2011?
58288.e: Wadi Rum in southern Jordan is known for its sandstone mountains and rock carvings. It was listed in 2011 as a mixed natural and cultural heritage site.
58288.m: Wadi Rum in Jordan is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

58289.q: Why are wells and oases often found in wadis?
a: Groundwater collects beneath the wadi floor
Wadis are always by the sea
It rains every day in wadis
58289.e: The rare floodwater seeps into the loose gravel of the wadi floor. Groundwater stays there longer and can be used through wells.
58289.m: Beneath dry wadis there is often usable groundwater.

a: A mountain rising alone from a plain
A mountain on an island in the sea
A hill made of glacial debris
58290.e: Inselbergs rise steeply and in isolation above a wide planation surface. They look like islands in a sea of plain.
58290.m: An inselberg rises like an island from a flat plain.

58291.q: Which famous inselberg rises from the plain in central Australia?
58291.e: Uluru, formerly Ayers Rock, rises about 350 metres above the flat surroundings. The term inselberg was coined around 1900 by the German geologist Wilhelm Bornhardt in East Africa.

58292.q: Who was Henry Ayers, after whom Uluru was named “Ayers Rock” in 1873?
58292.e: The surveyor William Gosse named the rock after Sir Henry Ayers, then Chief Secretary of South Australia. Today the official name is Uluru / Ayers Rock.
58292.m: The name Ayers Rock goes back to the politician Henry Ayers.

58293.q: How do the rock layers in Uluru lie today?
a: Horizontal, as when they were deposited
58293.e: The layers were once deposited horizontally and later tilted to about 85 degrees during mountain building. That is why the edges of the layers can be seen today as fine ribs on Uluru.
58293.m: In Uluru the rock layers stand almost vertically.

58294.q: What does deflation mean in geomorphology?
58294.e: In deflation, the wind lifts fine, loose material such as dust and sand from the ground and carries it away. The term comes from the Latin “deflare”, meaning to blow away.
58294.m: Deflation means the wind blows loose material away.

58295.q: What is the wearing away of rock by wind-driven sand grains called, as opposed to deflation?
58295.e: In corrasion, the wind acts like a sandblaster and grinds rocks down. In deflation, on the other hand, only loose material is blown away.
58295.m: Corrasion grinds rock down, deflation blows loose material away.

58296.q: Which surface is left behind when the wind blows all the fine material out of a mixture of gravel and fine material?
58296.e: The coarse stones are too heavy for the wind and stay where they are. They form a dense desert pavement that protects the ground beneath.
58296.m: Deflation leaves behind a protective desert pavement.

58297.q: What is the gravel desert that often forms through deflation called?
58297.e: Serir or reg is a gravel desert in which the wind has blown out the fine material. Erg is the sand desert, hamada the rock or stone desert.
58297.m: In a serir, mainly gravel is left after deflation.

58298.q: Which large depression in Egypt is an example of a hollow partly shaped by deflation?
58298.e: The Qattara Depression lies in Egypt’s Western Desert and reaches about 133 metres below sea level. Over a long time the wind blew out the weathered material.
58298.m: The Qattara Depression was blown out deeply by the wind.

58299.q: Which event in Switzerland shows that dust blown out by deflation is carried a long way?
a: The foehn brings rain to Ticino
The bise dries out the Swiss Plateau
Fog lies over the Swiss Plateau
58299.e: Storms in the Sahara lift fine dust high into the air. South winds carry it as far as the Alps, where it colours snow and sky yellowish to reddish.
58299.m: Saharan dust can travel thousands of kilometres to Switzerland.

58300.q: Which wind-deposited fine sediment is the counterpart to deflation and forms fertile soils?
58300.e: Fine dust blown out by the wind is deposited elsewhere as loess. Loess soils are among the most fertile farmland soils.
58300.m: Loess forms from dust that the wind has blown out elsewhere.

58301.q: What was the environmental disaster of the 1930s in the USA called, when wind blew away huge amounts of farmland soil?
58301.e: After droughts and intensive ploughing of the prairie, the soil was unprotected. Storms blew the topsoil away and many farming families had to move away.
58301.m: The Dust Bowl shows how destructive deflation can be on unprotected farmland.

58302.q: Which process mainly shapes the narrow base of a mushroom rock in the desert?
a: Sandblasting by wind near the ground
58302.e: The wind carries sand grains mainly close to the ground. There it acts like a sandblaster and grinds the base of the rock more than the upper part.
58302.m: A mushroom rock is ground away at its base by sand.

58303.q: Why is wind abrasion strongest close to the ground?
a: Most sand grains bounce close to the ground
The wind is fastest at the ground
The rock is always softer at the ground
The air is driest at the ground
58303.e: Heavy sand grains are lifted only a little by the wind. The grinding effect is therefore limited to a zone near the ground.
58303.m: Sand grains mostly fly low, so the wind grinds mainly at the bottom.

58304.q: Which difference in the rock helps a mushroom rock to form?
a: A hard top layer over softer rock
A soft top layer over hard rock
58304.e: A resistant layer at the top forms the cap. The softer rock beneath is worn away faster and forms the narrow stem.
58304.m: A hard cap over soft rock allows a mushroom rock to form.

58305.q: Which kind of weathering, besides the wind, can further weaken the base of mushroom rocks?
a: Salt weathering due to ground moisture
58305.e: Near the ground, the rock is often a little damper and saltier. Salt weathering loosens the rock there, which the wind can then remove more easily.
58305.m: Salt weathering near the ground helps shape the stem of a mushroom rock.

58306.q: In which Egyptian desert landscape are mushroom-shaped limestone rocks a well-known sight?
58306.e: The White Desert near the Farafra oasis is known for its white chalk rocks shaped by the wind. Many of them are shaped like mushrooms or animals.
58306.m: In Egypt’s White Desert, the wind shaped limestone rocks into mushrooms.

58307.q: Which similar-looking forms in Valais were not created by wind but by rain washing away soft moraine material?
a: The karren fields of the Schrattenfluh
The dripstones of the St Beatus Caves
58307.e: At Euseigne, large capstones protect the moraine material beneath them from rain. Tall pillars with a stone as a cap were left standing.
58307.m: The earth pyramids of Euseigne are pillars with a protective capstone.

58308.q: How are the long, streamlined rock ridges in deserts called yardangs formed?
a: By rivers in the rainy season
58308.e: Sand-laden wind grinds the rock in its direction. This creates ridges lying parallel to the wind direction, which, like mushroom rocks, are a form of wind erosion.
58308.m: Yardangs are rock ridges ground by the wind.

58309.q: Besides the river’s erosion, which geological process was crucial for the great depth of the Grand Canyon?
a: The uplift of the Colorado Plateau
58309.e: As the Colorado Plateau rose, the river cut deeper and deeper. This combination of uplift and downcutting created the gorge.
58309.m: Uplift of the plateau and downcutting by the river created the Grand Canyon.

58310.q: Who led the first documented boat expedition through the Grand Canyon in 1869?
58310.e: In 1869 the geologist John Wesley Powell travelled down the Green River and the Colorado River with a small group. On the way he explored the Grand Canyon.
58310.m: In 1869 John Wesley Powell made the first documented trip through the Grand Canyon.

58311.q: In which year was the Grand Canyon declared a national park of the USA?
58311.e: Grand Canyon National Park was founded in 1919. Since 1979 it has also been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
58311.m: The Grand Canyon has been a national park since 1919.

58312.q: Why do the walls of the Grand Canyon show a typical stepped profile?
a: Hard and soft layers weather differently
The river changed direction every year
58312.e: Resistant layers such as limestone and sandstone form steep walls. Softer shales weather faster and form gentler slopes.
58312.m: Layers of different hardness create the steps in the Grand Canyon.

58313.q: Where does the water of many wadis often end up after a flood?
a: In a basin with no outlet
58313.e: Many wadis never reach the sea because the water seeps away and evaporates on the way. It often collects in basins where salt pans (sabkhas) can form.
58313.m: Many wadis end in basins with no outlet in the middle of the desert.

58314.q: Which group of conglomerate rocks lies about 25 kilometres west of Uluru in the same national park?
58314.e: Kata Tjuta, also called the Olgas, consists of 36 dome-shaped rocks. Together with Uluru it forms Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park.
58314.m: Kata Tjuta lies in the same national park as Uluru.

58315.q: Roughly how long is the circumference of Uluru at its base?
58315.e: Uluru is about 3.6 kilometres long and almost 2 kilometres wide. Its circumference is about 9.4 kilometres.
58315.m: Walking around Uluru means walking about nine kilometres.

58316.q: Roughly how old are the oldest rocks at the bottom of the Grand Canyon?
58316.e: Right at the bottom of the Inner Gorge are metamorphic rocks such as the Vishnu Schist. They are about 1.7 billion years old.
58316.m: At the bottom of the Grand Canyon lie rocks about 1.7 billion years old.

58317.q: Why are fossils of sea creatures found in the limestone at the top rim of the Grand Canyon?
a: The area used to lie beneath a sea
Birds carried the animals from the Pacific
The Colorado River washed them upstream
A tsunami threw them onto the plateau
58317.e: The Kaibab Limestone at the rim of the gorge formed about 270 million years ago on the floor of a shallow sea. Later the area was uplifted and today lies over 2000 m high.
58317.m: Sea fossils high up show that the land was once under water.

58318.q: In the Grand Canyon, what is the boundary called where hundreds of millions of years of rock history are missing?
58318.e: At this unconformity, young sedimentary layers lie directly on much older basement rock. The rocks in between were eroded or never deposited.
58318.m: The Great Unconformity shows a huge gap in the sequence of rocks.

58319.e: Karst forms only in rocks that dissolve in water. These include carbonate rocks such as limestone and dolomite as well as sulphate and salt rocks.
58319.m: Karst forms only in rocks that water can dissolve.

58320.q: In which climate do inselbergs above planation surfaces typically form?
a: In the high mountains of the Alps
58320.e: In the savannas of the seasonally wet tropics, rock weathers deeply and is worn down over wide areas. Hard cores of rock are left standing as inselbergs.
58320.m: Inselbergs are typical of the savannas of the seasonally wet tropics.

58321.q: In which type of dune do the arms point into the wind, unlike a barchan?
58321.e: Parabolic dunes are often held in place at the arms by plants, while the middle part keeps moving. That is why their arms point into the wind.
58321.m: In a parabolic dune, the arms point into the wind.

58322.q: What are stones called that the wind has ground to give them sharp edges and smooth faces?
58322.e: Ventifacts form when sand-laden wind strikes a stone over a long time. Depending on the number of edges, they are called, for example, dreikanters (three-edged stones).
58322.m: Ventifacts are stones that sandy wind has ground into sharp edges.

58323.q: Roughly how high does Uluru rise above the surrounding plain?
58323.e: Uluru rises about 348 metres above the plain. Its summit is about 863 metres above sea level.
58323.m: Uluru rises about 350 metres above the plain.

58324.q: Which Aboriginal people are the traditional owners of Uluru?
58324.e: Uluru is a sacred place for the Anangu. Since 1985 the land has officially belonged to them again, and the park is managed jointly.
58324.m: The Anangu are the traditional owners of Uluru.

58325.q: What are the round limestone formations that form in small pools of water in caves called?
58325.e: A grain of sand or a small stone is moved about in the dripping water and coated all round with limestone. This is how smooth, rounded cave pearls grow.
58325.m: Cave pearls form when limestone is deposited all round a moving core.

58326.q: What is the weathering of granite into rounded, cushion-shaped blocks called?
58326.e: Granite weathers along its joints, with the edges of the blocks attacked most strongly. This creates rounded blocks that look like stacked woolsacks.
58326.m: In woolsack weathering, granite turns into round, cushion-shaped blocks.

58327.q: Which cross-section is typical of a glacial trough shaped by a glacier?
58327.e: A valley glacier scours the floor and sides at the same time and so widens the valley. This creates a U-shaped cross-section with a wide valley floor and steep walls.
58327.m: Glaciers form U-shaped valleys, rivers form V-shaped valleys.

58328.q: What is the gentler ledge above the steep walls of a glacial trough called?
58328.e: The trough shoulder lies above the trough wall and often marks the height of an older valley floor or the glacier surface. In the Alps, alpine pastures and villages are often found on it.
58328.m: Alpine pastures and mountain villages are often found on the trough shoulder.

58329.q: Why do hanging valleys open out high above the floor of a glacial trough?
a: The main glacier eroded deeper than the side glaciers
Side valleys were later lifted by tectonic forces
Rivers in side valleys deposit more debris
The main river has filled its bed with gravel
58329.e: The huge main glacier had more ice and therefore more erosive power than the small side glaciers. After the ice melted, the side valleys therefore end at a steep step high above the main valley.
58329.m: Hanging valleys show that the main glacier dug deeper.

58330.q: Which valley in the Bernese Oberland is a textbook example of a glacial trough with waterfalls from hanging valleys?
58330.e: The Lauterbrunnen Valley has almost vertical rock walls over which many streams from hanging valleys plunge, such as the Staubbach Falls. It is considered one of the most impressive glacial troughs in the Alps.
58330.m: The Lauterbrunnen Valley is a classic example of a glacial trough.

58331.q: What is meant by glacial overdeepening of a glacial trough?
a: The glacier scours basins deeper than the later valley exit
A river cuts deeply into the ground after the Ice Age
The valley floor sinks as limestone dissolves
A rockslide dams the valley to form a lake
58331.e: Under pressure, glaciers can also flow uphill and can therefore scour basins below the level of the valley exit. Such overdeepened basins often later fill with lakes or sediments.
58331.m: Glaciers can scour basins deeper than the valley exit.

58332.q: Which national park in California is famous for its ice-shaped glacial trough with granite walls?
58332.e: Yosemite Valley was widened into a glacial trough by Ice Age glaciers. Rock walls such as El Capitan and hanging valleys with waterfalls shape the scenery.
58332.m: Yosemite Valley is a glacial trough with high granite walls.

58333.q: What is a threshold of harder rock lying across a glacial trough, which the glacier could not completely wear away, called?
58333.e: Harder parts of the rock resist glacial erosion and remain as a rock bar across the valley. Behind it there is often an overdeepened basin with a lake or a plain.
58333.m: A rock bar is a hard rock threshold across a glacial trough.

58334.q: How can you tell the maximum height of the glacier surface during the Ice Age on the wall of a glacial trough?
58334.e: Below the trimline the rock has been polished smooth by the ice, above it it is jagged from frost weathering. The line shows how thick the ice once was.
58334.m: The trimline reveals the former height of the glacier ice.

58335.q: What is a cirque in glacial geomorphology?
a: An armchair-shaped hollow on a mountainside
A long hill of ground moraine
A ridge of debris in front of the glacier snout
58335.e: A cirque is a hollow scoured out by a small glacier, with a steep back wall and a flatter floor. It usually lies high up on mountainsides and is often where a valley glacier begins.
58335.m: A cirque looks like an armchair pressed into the mountain.

58336.q: What is a small lake that forms in the floor of a cirque after the ice has melted called?
58336.e: The glacier has overdeepened the cirque floor into a hollow. After the ice melts, water collects in this hollow to form a tarn.
58336.m: Many cirques today hold a small tarn.

58337.q: What is the raised rock edge at the exit of a cirque that dams the tarn called?
58337.e: Because the glacier in a cirque flows with a rotating motion, it scours the middle deeper than the exit. At the edge, a threshold of rock or moraine is left standing.
58337.m: The cirque lip dams the water in the cirque to form a lake.

58338.q: Which mountain shape forms when three or more cirques eat into a peak from different sides?
58338.e: When cirques cut back from several sides, sharp ridges and a pointed summit are left between them. This pyramid shape is called a horn.
58338.m: A horn forms when cirques eat into a peak from all sides.

58339.q: Which Swiss mountain is a well-known example of a horn?
58339.e: The Matterhorn has steep faces and sharp ridges carved out by cirques on several sides. It is therefore regarded worldwide as the classic example of a horn.
58339.m: The Matterhorn is a classic example of a horn.

58341.q: What is a small glacier called that only fills the hollow of a cirque and does not form a distinct tongue?
