58998.q: What is a society called in which over 21 percent of the population is 65 or older, as in Japan?
58998.e: According to a common classification, a society is ageing from 7 percent over 65, aged from 14 percent and super-aged from 21 percent.
58998.m: With over 21 percent over 65, Japan is a super-aged society.

58999.q: Roughly what was Japan's fertility rate in 2024?
58999.e: Japan's fertility rate fell to a record low of about 1.15 in 2024. This is far below replacement level.
58999.m: Japanese women have on average only slightly more than one child.

59000.q: What is a main reason why Japan's population hardly grows through immigration despite a labour shortage?
a: Its traditionally very restrictive immigration policy
The lack of airports and ports
A legal ban on Japanese people leaving the country
59000.e: For a long time Japan admitted only a few immigrants. The share of foreigners is much lower than in Switzerland, but has been rising in recent years.
59000.m: Japan has traditionally relied little on immigration.

59001.q: Which problem is particularly visible in rural regions of Japan?
a: Many empty houses and dying villages
A strong influx of young families to the countryside
A lack of cemeteries in small towns
59001.e: Young people move to cities such as Tokyo, and older people stay behind. In the 2023 survey, Japan counted about 9 million empty houses, called “akiya”.
59001.m: In the Japanese countryside, many houses stand empty.

59002.q: With which technology, among others, is Japan trying to make up for its shortage of care workers?
59002.e: Japan supports robots that help lift patients or keep older people company. This is meant to secure care despite fewer workers.
59002.m: Japan uses robots in care for the elderly.

59003.q: Roughly what is the median age of Japan's population?
59003.e: Half of the people in Japan are older than about 49. Japan therefore has one of the highest median ages in the world.
59003.m: Japan has one of the highest median ages in the world.

59004.q: What is an important economic consequence of ageing in Japan?
a: Rising costs for pensions and health
A sharply rising number of schoolchildren
59004.e: More and more pensioners receive benefits, while the number of people paying contributions falls. Social spending makes up a large part of the state budget.
59004.m: Ageing increases the costs of pensions and health in Japan.

59005.q: Why is Bangladesh particularly remarkable in population geography?
a: It is the most densely populated large country in the world
It is the least populated country in Asia
It has the oldest population in the world
It has the lowest population density in Asia
59005.e: Apart from city states and microstates such as Monaco or Singapore, no country has such a high population density as Bangladesh.
59005.m: Bangladesh is the most densely populated large country on Earth.

59006.q: Roughly what is the population density of Bangladesh?
59006.e: With about 170 million inhabitants on just under 150,000 km², that gives over 1100 inhabitants per km². Switzerland has about 220.
59006.m: In Bangladesh, over 1100 people live on one square kilometre.

59007.q: How do you calculate population density?
a: Number of inhabitants divided by area
Area divided by number of inhabitants
59007.e: Population density shows how many people live on average on one square kilometre. So you divide the number of inhabitants by the area.
59007.m: Population density is the number of inhabitants per square kilometre.

59008.q: Switzerland has about 9 million inhabitants on about 41,000 km². Roughly what is its population density?
59008.e: 9,000,000 ÷ 41,000 gives about 220 inhabitants per km². So Bangladesh is about five times more densely populated.
59008.m: Switzerland has about 220 inhabitants per square kilometre.

59009.q: Which natural condition makes the dense settlement of Bangladesh possible?
a: Fertile alluvial soils in the delta of the Ganges and Brahmaputra
Large oil deposits in high mountains
A dry desert climate with oases
Extensive coniferous forests in the lowlands
59009.e: Most of the country lies in the delta of the Ganges and Brahmaputra. The fertile soils and the monsoon allow several rice harvests a year.
59009.m: Fertile delta soils feed the many people in Bangladesh.

59010.q: Which hazard hits Bangladesh's dense population particularly hard?
59010.e: Large parts of the country lie only a few metres above sea level. Monsoon floods and cyclones threaten millions of people, and rising sea levels increase the risk.
59010.m: Bangladesh is severely threatened by floods and cyclones.

59011.q: What is the name of the capital and largest city of Bangladesh?
59011.e: With over 20 million people in its urban area, Dhaka is one of the most densely populated cities in the world.
59011.m: Dhaka is the capital of Bangladesh.

59012.q: How has Bangladesh's fertility rate developed since the 1970s?
a: It fell from over 6 to about 2 children per woman
It rose from 2 to over 6 children per woman
It stayed constant at about 4 children per woman
It fell from 3 to below 1 child per woman
59012.e: Thanks to family planning programmes, better education and health care, the fertility rate fell sharply. Bangladesh is regarded as a success story for this.
59012.m: Bangladesh has greatly lowered its birth rate in 50 years.

59013.q: Roughly how many inhabitants did Bangladesh have in the 2022 census?
59013.e: The 2022 census counted just under 170 million inhabitants. This puts Bangladesh among the ten most populous countries in the world.

a: Deaths in the first year of life per 1000 live births
Deaths before the 5th birthday per 100 children
59014.e: Infant mortality counts the children who die before their first birthday, per 1000 live births.
59014.m: Infant mortality counts deaths in the first year of life.

59015.q: Roughly what is infant mortality in Switzerland?
59015.e: In Switzerland, about 3 in 1000 babies die in their first year of life. Around 1900 it was still well over 100.
59015.m: In Switzerland, almost all babies survive their first year.

59016.q: Why is infant mortality seen as an important development indicator?
a: It reflects health care, hygiene and nutrition
It shows the number of hospitals per inhabitant
It measures the share of women in politics
It gives the gross domestic product per person
59016.e: Babies are very sensitive to bad water, malnutrition and a lack of medical help. That is why the figure says a lot about living conditions.
59016.m: Infant mortality shows how well a country cares for mothers and children.

59017.q: According to the UN, roughly what was global infant mortality around 2023?
59017.e: According to the UN group on child mortality, the global figure around 2023 was about 27. In 1990 it was more than twice as high.
59017.m: Infant mortality worldwide has more than halved since 1990.

59018.q: Which simple treatment saves many lives when babies have diarrhoea?
a: Oral rehydration solution made of water, salt and sugar
A cold shower after every meal
59018.e: The solution replaces lost fluid and salts. It is cheap and has saved millions of children from dying of dehydration.
59018.m: A solution of water, salt and sugar saves children with diarrhoea.

59019.q: What is meant by neonatal mortality?
a: Deaths in the first 28 days of life
Deaths in the first 12 months of life
59019.e: Neonatal mortality covers the first four weeks of life. The risk of dying is highest during this time.
59019.m: Neonatal mortality covers the first 28 days of life.

59020.q: What relationship often exists between infant mortality and the birth rate?
a: When infant mortality falls, the birth rate usually falls later too
When infant mortality falls, the birth rate rises permanently
The two figures are completely independent
High infant mortality lowers the birth rate
59020.e: When parents can be sure their children will survive, they usually want fewer children. This is a key element of the demographic transition.
59020.m: When more children survive, families later have fewer children.

59021.q: In a country, 50,000 children are born alive and 1500 die in their first year. What is the infant mortality rate?
59021.e: 1500 ÷ 50,000 gives 0.03. Multiplied by 1000, that is 30 deaths per 1000 live births.
59021.m: Infant mortality is calculated per 1000 live births.

59022.q: Which measure greatly reduced infant mortality worldwide in the 20th century?
a: The invention of the fridge for drinks
59022.e: Vaccinations, for example against measles, diphtheria and whooping cough, protect babies from deadly diseases. Together with clean water they greatly lowered mortality.
59022.m: Vaccinations protect babies from deadly diseases.

59023.q: Which region of the world has the highest infant mortality?
59023.e: In countries such as Sierra Leone, Niger or Somalia, many more babies die than the world average. The main reasons are infections, malnutrition and a lack of care at birth.
59023.m: Most infant deaths occur in sub-Saharan Africa.

59024.q: Why do rich countries often recruit immigrants for insecure, low-paid jobs?
a: Hardly any local people can be found for these jobs
Immigrants are not allowed to pay taxes
Local people are not allowed to take these jobs
Immigrants do not need any training
59024.e: In industrialised countries, many local people avoid badly paid and insecure work. That is why there is a constant need for immigrants, for example in construction or agriculture.
59024.m: Demand in the destination country also drives migration.

59025.q: Which of the following is a typical pull factor of migration?
a: A labour shortage in the destination country
Drought in the country of origin
Persecution in the country of origin
High unemployment in the country of origin
59025.e: Pull factors are attractive conditions at the destination. If workers are lacking there, job vacancies attract immigrants.
59025.m: Pull factors attract people to a new place.

59026.q: What are causes such as war or poverty that drive people away from their country of origin called?
59026.e: Push factors drive people away from where they live. Pull factors such as good jobs attract them to a new place.
59026.m: Push factors drive people away, pull factors attract them.

59027.q: Which category did Everett S. Lee add to the factors in the area of origin and destination in his 1966 migration model?
59027.e: Lee stressed that between origin and destination there are obstacles such as distance, cost or border laws. Personal factors also play a role.
59027.m: Obstacles along the way influence whether people really migrate.

59028.q: What is migration that is made easier by relatives and friends who have already emigrated called?
59028.e: In chain migration, pioneers help those who follow with information, accommodation and work. In this way, communities from the same region of origin form at the destination.
59028.m: Networks of relatives make further emigration easier.

59029.q: What does the “migration hump” theory say about poor countries whose incomes are starting to rise?
59029.e: Rising incomes allow more people to afford the costs of emigrating. Only at higher levels of wealth does emigration fall again.
59029.m: A little more wealth can at first increase emigration.

59030.q: Which cause does neoclassical migration theory put at the centre?
59030.e: According to neoclassical theory, workers move from regions with low wages to regions with high wages. In the long run, migration evens out the wage differences.
59030.m: Neoclassical theory explains migration mainly by wage gaps.

59031.q: Why do families in poorer countries often send one member abroad to work?
a: To spread the family's income risk
To avoid paying taxes at home
Because the law there requires it
To sell the farm at home
59031.e: If the harvest fails at home or a job is lost, money from abroad keeps the household secure. Experts therefore often see migration as a joint family strategy.
59031.m: Families often send one member abroad to spread their risk.

59032.q: With which country did Switzerland sign an agreement on recruiting workers in 1948?
59032.e: The 1948 agreement regulated the immigration of Italian workers, who were needed in construction, industry and the hotel and restaurant trade. A similar agreement with Spain followed in 1961.
59032.m: After the Second World War, Italy was the most important country of origin for workers in Switzerland.

59033.q: What is the renewed increase in population in city centres after a period of people moving out to the surrounding area called?
59033.e: In reurbanisation, more people move back into city centres, for example because of short distances and cultural offerings. The city of Zurich has been growing again in this way since around 2000.
59033.m: Cities can grow again after a period of shrinking.

59034.q: What is the movement of people from rural areas to cities called?
59034.e: Rural exodus is often caused by a lack of jobs and services in the countryside. It is an important driver of urbanisation in many countries.
59034.m: Rural exodus makes cities grow and villages shrink.

59035.q: What is the shift of population from the core city to the surrounding urban area called?
59035.e: In suburbanisation, people move to the suburbs, for example because of cheaper housing or more green space. In Switzerland many municipalities in urban areas grew strongly in this way.
59035.m: In suburbanisation, the suburbs around cities grow.

59036.q: Which internal migration in US history is known as the “Great Migration”?
a: African Americans moved from the South to the North and West
Settlers moved to California in the gold rush
Pensioners moved to Florida in large numbers
Farmers moved from Texas to Alaska
59036.e: Between about 1910 and 1970, around six million African Americans left the southern states. They fled racial segregation and looked for industrial work in cities such as Chicago or Detroit.
59036.m: The Great Migration changed the population of many cities in the northern USA.

59037.q: Which event in the 1930s triggered a large migration from the Great Plains to California?
a: The dust storms of the Dust Bowl
A once-in-a-century flood on the Hudson
59037.e: Drought and poor farming methods led to huge dust storms. Hundreds of thousands of impoverished farming families therefore moved west.
59037.m: The Dust Bowl shows how environmental damage forces people to migrate.

59038.q: Which internal migration particularly shaped Germany after reunification in 1990?
a: Migration from East to West Germany
People moving from the Ruhr to Saxony
59038.e: After 1990, mainly young people moved west for better jobs. As a result, many East German regions lost inhabitants and aged quickly.
59038.m: After reunification, many East German regions lost young people to the West.

59039.q: What is a consequence of young people moving away from many remote Swiss mountain valleys?
a: Ageing population and village shops closing
A sharp rise in pupil numbers
A housing shortage in mountain villages
59039.e: When young people move to the centres for training and work, mainly older people stay behind. Schools, shops and post offices lose their customers as a result.
59039.m: Migration away makes many mountain villages age.

59040.q: What is migration called in which people move step by step from a village via small towns to a big city?
59040.e: Early migration researchers already observed that many people do not move directly to the big city. They migrate in several stages via smaller places in between.
59040.m: Step migration leads from the countryside to the city step by step.

59041.q: What was the name of Indonesia's state programme that moved people from the densely populated island of Java to other islands?
59041.e: With Transmigrasi, Indonesia wanted to reduce overpopulation on Java and develop other islands. However, the programme also led to conflicts and forest clearing.
59041.m: Indonesia tried to relieve Java through state resettlement.

59042.q: What is the sponsorship system called that ties the residence of foreign workers in Gulf states to an employer?
59042.e: Under the kafala system, the employer is the worker's sponsor. For a long time, changing jobs or leaving the country was therefore only possible with the employer's consent.
59042.m: The kafala system makes migrant workers highly dependent on their employers.

59043.q: From which world region do most migrant workers in the Gulf states come?
59043.e: Most workers come from India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Nepal. They work mainly in construction, in the service sector and as domestic workers.
59043.m: South Asia is the most important region of origin for workers in the Gulf.

59044.q: Roughly what share of Qatar's population are foreign nationals?
59044.e: In Qatar, only about one tenth of the inhabitants hold Qatari citizenship. The vast majority are foreign workers and their families.
59044.m: In Qatar, the local people are a small minority.

59045.q: Which event triggered the strong labour migration to the Gulf states from the 1970s?
a: The sharp rise in oil prices from 1973
The building of the Suez Canal
The end of the Cold War
The founding of the Arab League
59045.e: The greatly increased oil revenues financed a huge building boom. Because the local population was small, the states brought in millions of foreign workers.
59045.m: Oil wealth made the Gulf states magnets for labour migration.

59046.q: Which major sporting event brought the working conditions of foreign construction workers in Qatar to the world's attention?
59046.e: Stadiums, roads and hotels were built for the tournament, mainly by migrant workers. Human rights organisations criticised the heat, wage theft and deaths on building sites.
59046.m: The World Cup in Qatar drew attention to the situation of migrant workers.

59047.q: Which Indian state has been especially strongly shaped by labour migration to the Gulf states for decades?
59047.e: Since the 1970s, a great many people from Kerala in south-west India have worked in the Gulf. Their money transfers shape spending, house building and education there.
59047.m: Kerala is closely linked to labour migration to the Gulf.

59048.q: How many states belong to the Gulf Cooperation Council, which includes the main destination countries of this labour migration?
59048.e: The members are Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman. All six states depend heavily on foreign workers.
59048.m: The Gulf Cooperation Council consists of six states.

59049.q: Which practice towards migrant workers in the Gulf states do human rights organisations criticise most often?
a: The obligation to give paid holidays
59049.e: Although it is banned in many places, employers often keep the passports. The workers can then neither quit nor leave the country.
59049.m: Without a passport, migrant workers are at the mercy of their employer.

59050.q: Which country introduced a minimum wage in 2021 that the International Labour Organization called the first non-discriminatory minimum wage in the Gulf region?
59050.e: In March 2021 Qatar brought in a general minimum wage that applies to all workers regardless of nationality. The ILO praised it as the first of its kind in the region.
59050.m: Reforms in Qatar set standards for the Gulf region.

a: Money that migrants send to relatives in their country of origin
World Bank loans to poor countries
59051.e: Remittances are private money transfers sent home by migrants. There they often pay for food, school fees, health and house building.
59051.m: Remittances link migrants financially with their families.

59052.q: According to the World Bank, roughly how much money flowed as remittances to low and middle-income countries in 2024?
59052.e: The World Bank estimated officially recorded remittances in 2024 at about 685 billion US dollars. The real amount is probably even higher because of informal channels.
59052.m: Remittances are a huge flow of money into poorer countries.

59053.q: According to the World Bank, which country received the most remittances in 2024?
59053.e: In 2024 India received about 129 billion US dollars from its citizens abroad. That is the highest amount in the world.
59053.m: India is the largest recipient of remittances.

59054.q: According to the World Bank, which country had the highest share of remittances in its gross domestic product in 2024?
59054.e: In Tajikistan, remittances were equal to about 45 percent of GDP in 2024. Many Tajiks work mainly in Russia.
59054.m: Some economies depend heavily on money from their emigrants.

59055.q: According to the World Bank (2024), how do remittances to low and middle-income countries compare with other capital flows?
a: They exceed direct investment and development aid combined
They are smaller than development aid
They are about the same as customs revenue
They are only a fraction of direct investment
59055.e: According to the World Bank, remittances in 2024 were larger than foreign direct investment and official development aid combined. That makes them one of the most important external sources of finance.
59055.m: Private money transfers clearly exceed government development aid.

59056.q: What is the traditional informal money transfer system based on trust between money dealers called?
59056.e: In the hawala system, you pay money to a dealer and a partner in the destination country pays out the amount, without the money physically travelling. It is cheap and fast but hard to control.
59056.m: Hawala works through trust rather than through banks.

59057.q: According to the UN Sustainable Development Goals, to what level should the transaction costs of remittances be reduced by 2030?
59057.e: Target 10.c of the 2030 Agenda calls for costs below 3 percent of the amount sent. Today, fees in many corridors are still considerably higher.
59057.m: Lower transfer fees mean more money reaches families.

59058.q: Which possible downside of high remittances do experts mention for receiving countries?
a: Dependence on other countries and less pressure for reform
59058.e: If a country lives largely on money transfers, the pressure to create its own jobs can fall. The economy also becomes vulnerable to crises in the destination countries.
59058.m: Remittances help, but they can also create dependence.

59059.q: In the Philippines, what are the workers employed abroad, whose remittances are very important for the economy, called?
59059.e: Millions of Filipinos work as Overseas Filipino Workers, for example in care or on ships. The state actively promotes and organises this labour migration.
59059.m: The Philippines deliberately promotes its citizens working abroad.

59060.q: Besides refugees, for which group of people has the UNHCR also been given a protection mandate?
59060.e: The UN General Assembly also gave the UNHCR the task of preventing statelessness and protecting stateless people. Prisoners of war, on the other hand, are looked after by the ICRC.
59060.m: The UNHCR also stands up for people without a nationality.

59061.q: In which year was the UNHCR founded by the UN General Assembly?
59061.e: The General Assembly decided to found it in December 1950, and work began in January 1951. Originally it was only meant to help refugees in Europe for a few years.
59061.m: The UNHCR was meant as temporary help and still exists today.

59062.q: How many times has the UNHCR received the Nobel Peace Prize?
59062.e: The UNHCR was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1954 and 1981. Its work for refugees worldwide was honoured.
59062.m: The UNHCR has won the Nobel Peace Prize twice.

59063.q: In which year was the Geneva Refugee Convention, the basis of the UNHCR's work, adopted?
59063.e: The Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees was adopted in Geneva on 28 July 1951. It defines who counts as a refugee and what rights they have.
59063.m: The Geneva Refugee Convention is the basic law of refugee protection.

59064.q: What is the principle that refugees must not be sent back to a country where they face persecution called?
59064.e: The ban on sending people back is in Article 33 of the Geneva Refugee Convention. It is seen as the core of international refugee protection.
59064.m: No one may be sent back to a country where they face persecution.

59065.q: On which date is the UN's World Refugee Day held each year?
59065.e: The UN General Assembly set World Refugee Day on 20 June, first held in 2001. It draws attention to the situation of refugees worldwide.
59065.m: On 20 June, the situation of refugees is in the spotlight.

59066.q: According to the UNHCR, how many people worldwide were forcibly displaced at the end of 2024?
59066.e: The “Global Trends” report gives about 123.2 million forcibly displaced people for the end of 2024. These include refugees, asylum seekers and people displaced within their own country.
59066.m: Over a hundred million people worldwide have been forced to flee.

59067.q: What did the 1967 New York Protocol change about the Geneva Refugee Convention?
a: It removed the time and geographical limits
It abolished the right of asylum in Europe
It handed refugee protection to NATO
It limited protection to war refugees
59067.e: Originally the Convention applied only to events before 1951 and could be limited to Europe. The Protocol made it a protection instrument valid worldwide.
59067.m: Since 1967, refugee protection has applied without limits of time or place.

59068.q: For which group of refugees is a separate UN agency responsible instead of the UNHCR?
59068.e: Since 1949 the agency UNRWA has been responsible for Palestine refugees in the Middle East. The UNHCR looks after almost all other groups of refugees.
59068.m: Palestine refugees have their own UN agency.

59069.q: How is the UNHCR mainly financed?
a: By voluntary contributions from states and donors
By compulsory contributions from the UN budget
By fees paid by asylum seekers
59069.e: Only a very small part of the budget comes from the regular UN budget. Almost everything is voluntary contributions from governments, the EU, companies and private individuals.
59069.m: The UNHCR depends on voluntary donations.

59070.q: What fundamentally distinguishes internally displaced people from refugees as defined by the Geneva Refugee Convention?
a: They have not crossed an international border
They flee only from natural disasters
59070.e: Internally displaced people had to leave their homes but stayed in their own country. That is why the Refugee Convention does not apply to them.
59070.m: Internally displaced people are displaced within their own country.

59071.q: According to the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC), how many internally displaced people were there worldwide at the end of 2024?
59071.e: The IDMC counted about 83.4 million internally displaced people at the end of 2024, more than ever before. The 80 million mark was passed for the first time.
59071.m: The number of internally displaced people reached a record in 2024.

59072.q: Which UN document from 1998 sums up the rights of internally displaced people?
a: The Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
59072.e: The Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement bring together existing human rights for internally displaced people. They are not binding, but they are widely recognised internationally.
59072.m: The UN Guiding Principles of 1998 protect internally displaced people.

59073.q: What does the African Union's 2009 Kampala Convention regulate?
a: The protection of internally displaced people
The protection of wildlife in national parks
59073.e: The Kampala Convention is the first regionally binding agreement specifically for internally displaced people. It came into force in 2012.
59073.m: With the Kampala Convention, Africa created binding law for internally displaced people.

59074.q: Which monitoring centre of the Norwegian Refugee Council collects worldwide figures on internally displaced people every year?
59074.e: The Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre was founded in 1998 and is based in Geneva. Every year it publishes the “Global Report on Internal Displacement”.
59074.m: The IDMC is the most important source of data on internal displacement.

59075.q: Which two main causes of internal displacement do the statistics distinguish?
59075.e: Displacement caused by conflict often lasts many years. Disasters such as floods or cyclones cause a great many, mostly shorter displacements every year.
59075.m: War and disasters are the main reasons for internal displacement.

59076.q: According to the IDMC, which country had the most people internally displaced by conflict at the end of 2024?
59076.e: Because of the war that broke out in 2023, about 11.6 million people in Sudan were internally displaced at the end of 2024. That is the highest number ever recorded for a single country.
59076.m: The war in Sudan caused the world's largest internal displacement crisis.

59077.q: Under international law, who has the main responsibility for protecting internally displaced people?
59077.e: Because internally displaced people stay in their own country, its government is responsible for them. International organisations only help in addition.
59077.m: Internally displaced people are first and foremost their own state's responsibility.

59078.q: Why are internally displaced people often particularly hard to protect?
a: They remain under the power of the state they are partly fleeing from
Legally they are classed as tourists
They are not allowed to accept help
59078.e: If their own government is a party to the conflict, it often does not protect displaced people. Aid organisations are also not always given access.
59078.m: Displaced people who do not cross a border often remain unprotected.

59079.q: What is the theory called that the prospect of emigrating motivates more people in the country of origin to get higher education?
59079.e: Because not all trained people actually emigrate, the number of qualified people in the country of origin can rise overall. Oded Stark and Andrew Mountford, among others, put forward this theory.
59079.m: Under some conditions, emigration can also boost education in the country of origin.

59080.q: What is a country's gain from the immigration of highly qualified people called?
59080.e: Brain gain is the counterpart of brain drain. Destination countries benefit from skilled workers whose training they did not pay for.
59080.m: What one country loses as brain drain, another gains as brain gain.

59081.q: What is the repeated movement of skilled workers called, in which knowledge also flows back to the country of origin?
59081.e: In brain circulation, skilled workers return or keep close contacts with home. In this way both countries benefit from the knowledge.
59081.m: Circulating skilled workers bring knowledge in both directions.

59082.q: What does the term “brain waste” mean?
a: Qualified migrants work below their level of training
Students drop out of their studies
Skilled workers emigrate to neighbouring countries
59082.e: If, for example, a trained doctor works as a cleaner, her knowledge is lost. The cause is often that foreign qualifications are not recognised.
59082.m: Brain waste wastes the qualifications of immigrants.

59083.q: For which emigration was the term “brain drain” originally coined in the 1960s?
a: British scientists moving to the USA
59083.e: The British Royal Society used the expression for the emigration of researchers to North America. Only later was it applied mainly to developing countries.
59083.m: The term brain drain first arose in Great Britain.

59084.q: Which organisation adopted a code of practice on the international recruitment of health personnel in 2010?
59084.e: The WHO code is meant to prevent rich countries from deliberately recruiting doctors and nurses from countries with staff shortages. It is voluntary.
59084.m: The WHO wants to prevent poor countries from losing their health workers.

59085.q: What is the EU residence permit for highly qualified workers from non-EU countries called?
59085.e: The EU Blue Card was introduced in 2009 to attract skilled workers. It is valid in most EU member states.
59085.m: With the Blue Card, the EU tries to attract skilled workers.

59086.q: According to the FMH doctors' statistics, what share of doctors working in Switzerland have a foreign qualification (as of 2024)?
59086.e: About two fifths of doctors in Switzerland obtained their qualification abroad, most of them in Germany. Switzerland thus benefits from training in other countries.
59086.m: The Swiss health system depends heavily on foreign skilled workers.

59087.q: What consequence can brain drain have for the health system of a country of origin?
a: A shortage of doctors and nurses
59087.e: When trained staff go abroad, they are missing in hospitals and health centres. Rural regions of poor countries are particularly affected.
59087.m: Skilled workers who emigrate leave gaps in care.

59088.q: What did the UN Human Rights Committee establish in principle in 2020 in the case of Ioane Teitiota from Kiribati?
a: Effects of climate change can make deportation unlawful
Climate migrants automatically count as refugees
Island states must resettle their inhabitants
New Zealand must take in all Pacific islanders
59088.e: Teitiota lost his case against New Zealand, but the Committee stated that life-threatening effects of climate change can in principle forbid deportations. This is seen as a ground-breaking decision.
59088.m: The Teitiota case opened a door to protecting people displaced by climate change.

59089.q: Which Pacific island state signed an agreement with Australia in 2023 offering up to 280 people a year the chance to live there because of climate change?
59089.e: Under the Falepili Union, up to 280 people from Tuvalu a year receive the right to live in Australia. The flat atoll is severely threatened by rising sea levels.
59089.m: Tuvalu secures its citizens a way out from the rising sea.

59090.q: According to the World Bank report “Groundswell” (2021), how many people could move within their own country because of climate change by 2050?
59090.e: In the worst-case scenario, the report expects up to 216 million internal climate migrants in six world regions. Rapid climate action could greatly reduce the number.
59090.m: By 2050, climate change could force hundreds of millions of people to move.

59091.q: What form does environmental migration usually take?
59091.e: Most of those affected move short distances, often to nearby cities. Many lack the money and papers for long journeys.
59091.m: Climate migration mostly takes place within a country's own borders.

59092.q: Which city in Bangladesh is a main destination for people leaving their villages because of floods and salty soils?
59092.e: Many people from the coastal and river areas of Bangladesh move to the capital Dhaka. There they often live in informal settlements.
59092.m: Bangladesh's capital is also growing because of climate migration.

59093.q: On which island did Kiribati buy land in 2014, partly as a precaution against the effects of rising sea levels?
59093.e: Kiribati bought about 20 square kilometres of land on the Fijian island of Vanua Levu. It is meant to secure food supplies and provide space in an emergency.
59093.m: Kiribati is preparing for the case that its atolls become uninhabitable.

59094.q: Which lake in Africa has shrunk greatly since the 1960s, increasing migration and conflict in the region?
59094.e: The area of Lake Chad shrank massively because of droughts and irrigation. Fishermen and farmers lost their livelihoods and moved away.
59094.m: Shrinking Lake Chad shows how environmental change drives people away.

59095.q: Which is an example of a slow-onset environmental event that can trigger migration?
59095.e: Desertification worsens living conditions over years until people move away. Sudden events such as storms, on the other hand, drive people away all at once.
59095.m: Gradual environmental changes can also force people to migrate.

59096.q: What does the Greek word “diaspora” literally mean?
59096.e: In Greek, diaspora means scattering. It refers to communities living scattered outside their area of origin.
59096.m: A diaspora is a community scattered across the world.

59097.q: To which population group did the term diaspora originally refer?
a: Jews outside the Land of Israel
59097.e: The term was first used for the Jewish communities after the Babylonian exile. Today it is used for many groups.
59097.m: The Jewish diaspora is the historical model of every diaspora.

59098.q: Which event led to massive emigration from Ireland from 1845?
59098.e: Potato blight destroyed the harvests and about a million people died. About as many emigrated, mainly to North America and Great Britain.
59098.m: The famine created a large Irish diaspora.

59099.q: Which people has a diaspora considerably larger than the population of its own state, partly as a result of the genocide from 1915?
59099.e: After the genocide in the Ottoman Empire, many survivors fled abroad. Today more Armenians live outside Armenia than inside it.
59099.m: The Armenian diaspora is larger than Armenia's population.

59100.q: What are the Swiss living abroad often called?
59100.e: Alongside the four language regions, the Swiss abroad are known as the “Fifth Switzerland”. The name stresses their connection to their homeland.
59100.m: The Swiss abroad form the Fifth Switzerland.

59101.q: According to the statistics on the Swiss abroad, roughly how many Swiss citizens lived abroad at the end of 2024?
59101.e: At the end of 2024, about 826,700 Swiss citizens lived abroad, 1.6 percent more than the year before. That is just over a tenth of all Swiss citizens.
59101.m: A significant part of the Swiss population lives abroad.

59102.q: In which country do most Swiss abroad live?
59102.e: France has long been the most important country of residence for the Swiss abroad. About two thirds of all Swiss abroad live in Europe.
59102.m: Neighbouring France is home to the largest Swiss community abroad.

59103.q: What is the main historical cause of the African diaspora in the Americas?
a: The search for gold in California
The building of the Panama Canal
59103.e: From the 16th to the 19th century, millions of Africans were forcibly taken to the Americas. Their descendants form a large diaspora today.
59103.m: The African diaspora in the Americas arose through forced deportation.

59104.q: What are ways of life called in which migrants keep close ties with both their country of origin and their destination country over the long term?
59104.e: Transnational migrants live in two worlds at the same time, for example through travel, money transfers and social media. Diaspora communities are often organised transnationally.
59104.m: Many migrants today live between two countries.

59105.q: Roughly how long is the border between Mexico and the USA?
59105.e: The border is about 3145 km long and stretches from the Pacific to the Gulf of Mexico. It crosses deserts, mountains and river valleys.
59105.m: The border between Mexico and the USA is over 3000 kilometres long.

59106.q: Which river forms the border between Mexico and the USA for about 2000 km?
59106.e: The Rio Grande, called Río Bravo del Norte in Mexico, separates Texas from Mexico. It forms the border as far as its mouth in the Gulf of Mexico.
59106.m: In Texas, the border runs along the Rio Grande.

59107.q: Which 1848 treaty laid the foundation for today's border after the Mexican-American War?
59107.e: With it, Mexico gave up large areas such as California and parts of New Mexico to the USA. The Rio Grande was recognised as the border with Texas.
59107.m: The 1848 treaty moved the border far to the south.

59108.q: Through which land purchase did the border essentially get its present course in 1853?
59108.e: The USA bought an area in the south of today's Arizona and New Mexico from Mexico. It was meant to make building a railway to California easier.
59108.m: With the Gadsden Purchase, today's border was almost complete.

59109.q: Between which two cities is the busiest border crossing between the USA and Mexico?
59109.e: The San Ysidro crossing connects San Diego with Tijuana. Tens of thousands of vehicles and pedestrians cross the border there every day.
59109.m: The busiest border crossing is between San Diego and Tijuana.

59110.q: Which Mexican city lies directly opposite El Paso in Texas?
59110.e: El Paso and Ciudad Juárez together form a cross-border urban area. Many people commute across the border every day.
59110.m: Border cities such as El Paso and Ciudad Juárez are closely intertwined.

59111.q: What was the programme called with which the USA recruited Mexican workers, mainly for agriculture, from 1942 to 1964?
59111.e: Through the Bracero Program, millions of work contracts were made with Mexicans. It began because of the labour shortage in the Second World War.
59111.m: The Bracero Program encouraged legal labour migration from Mexico.

59112.q: What are the assembly plants in the Mexican border area that produce for the US market with customs advantages called?
59112.e: Maquiladoras import parts duty-free, assemble them with cheap labour and export the products. They attract many internal migrants to border towns.
59112.m: Maquiladoras turned the border area into an industrial location.

59113.q: Roughly how many legal border crossings does the border between Mexico and the USA see each year?
59113.e: With about 350 million legal crossings a year, it is considered one of the most crossed borders in the world. There is especially heavy traffic between San Diego and Tijuana.
59113.m: Despite fences, the border is one of the busiest in the world.

59114.q: What is the Chinese household registration system that disadvantages migrant workers in cities called?
59114.e: The hukou ties rights to school, health care and social benefits to the place of registration. Anyone moving from the countryside to a city often has fewer rights there.
59114.m: The hukou system separates the urban and rural population legally.

59115.q: How many migrant workers did China's statistics office count in 2024?
59115.e: The National Bureau of Statistics counted about 299.7 million migrant workers in 2024. That is about a fifth of China's population.
59115.m: China has hundreds of millions of migrant workers.

59116.q: What does the Chinese term for migrant workers, “nongmingong”, literally mean?
59116.e: Nongmingong is made up of the words for farmer and worker. The term shows that these people are still officially counted as rural population.
59116.m: Chinese migrant workers are still officially counted as farmers.

59117.q: What is the yearly wave of travel called when millions of migrant workers go back to their villages for Chinese New Year?
59117.e: During Chunyun, billions of journeys take place within a few weeks. It is considered the largest yearly movement of people in the world.
59117.m: For New Year, China's migrant workers return home in huge numbers.

59118.q: In China, what are children called who stay with their grandparents in the countryside while their parents work in cities?
59118.e: Tens of millions of these children (liushou ertong) often see their parents only once a year. Experts are worried about their education and mental health.
59118.m: In China, migrant work separates many children from their parents.

59119.q: Which special economic zone, founded in 1980, became one of the most important destinations for Chinese migrant workers?
59119.e: Shenzhen grew from a small town into a metropolis of millions with many export factories. A large part of its population has moved there from elsewhere.
59119.m: Thanks to migration, Shenzhen became a megacity.

59120.q: In which direction has the main migration of Chinese migrant workers traditionally gone?
a: From the inland provinces to the coastal regions
From the coastal regions to Tibet
From the cities to the villages
59120.e: Workers from provinces such as Sichuan, Henan or Anhui moved to the industrial centres on the coast, for example in the Pearl River Delta. There was more work and higher wages there.
59120.m: China's migrant workers moved mainly from the interior to the coast.

59121.q: Roughly what was the average monthly income of Chinese migrant workers in 2024?
59121.e: According to the statistics office, it was 4961 yuan in 2024, which is about 690 US dollars. Income rose by 3.8 percent compared with the previous year.
59121.m: Migrant workers in China earn considerably less than many city dwellers.

59122.q: What was the Chinese hukou system mainly meant to control when it was introduced?
a: Migration from the countryside to the cities
The number of children per family
59122.e: The 1958 regulation tied people to their place of registration and was meant to control movement into the cities. Since the economic reforms, the system has been relaxed step by step.
59122.m: For decades, household registration has controlled internal migration in China.

59123.q: Which population threshold does the UN usually use for a megacity in its urbanisation reports?
59123.e: In the “World Urbanization Prospects”, urban areas with at least 10 million inhabitants count as megacities. The threshold is a convention, not a natural limit.
59123.m: The UN counts urban areas of 10 million people or more as megacities.

59124.q: According to UN data, which two cities were the only megacities around 1950?
59124.e: Around 1950, only the urban areas of New York and Tokyo passed the 10 million mark. Today there are several dozen megacities.
59124.m: Around 1950 there were only two megacities, New York and Tokyo.

59125.q: Which megacity in Bangladesh is one of the most densely populated cities in the world?
59125.e: Dhaka is the capital of Bangladesh and is growing very fast through migration from the countryside. Many millions of people live there in a small space.
59125.m: Dhaka is one of the densest megacities in the world.

59126.q: Which megacity is considered the largest French-speaking city in the world?
59126.e: Kinshasa, the capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, has considerably more inhabitants than Paris. French is the official language there.
59126.m: Kinshasa is now larger than any other French-speaking city.

59127.q: Which megacity is the largest urban area in South America?
59127.e: Greater São Paulo has over 20 million inhabitants. It is the economic centre of Brazil.
59127.m: São Paulo is the largest urban region in South America.

59128.q: According to UN-Habitat, which term describes an urban area with over 20 million inhabitants?
59128.e: UN-Habitat introduced the term “metacity” for urban areas with over 20 million people. It stands for a step up from a megacity.
59128.m: A metacity is a giant city with over 20 million inhabitants.

59129.q: Which factor drives the growth of many megacities in the Global South more strongly today than was often assumed in the early phase?
59129.e: Besides migration from the countryside to the city, the surplus of births over deaths among people already living in the city contributes a large part of the growth. This is especially true for cities in Africa.
59129.m: Megacities grow through migration and a surplus of births.

59130.q: What is the part of the economy in megacities that runs without state registration, taxes or social security called?
59130.e: Street trading, small workshops or casual work are typical activities in the informal sector. In many megacities of the South, a large share of people work there.
59130.m: Many people in megacities work in the informal sector.

59131.q: What problem arises in megacities such as Jakarta or Mexico City from taking too much groundwater?
59131.e: If too much groundwater is pumped out, the layers of soil compact and the surface sinks. As a result, parts of Jakarta are sinking by several centimetres a year.
59131.m: Taking too much groundwater makes the ground under cities sink.

59132.q: What distinguishes a metropolitan region from just the core city?
a: A functionally linked area of core city and surroundings
A city with exactly one million inhabitants
59132.e: A metropolitan region includes the core city and the surrounding area, which is closely linked to it by commuter flows, the economy and infrastructure. Municipal boundaries play a minor role here.
59132.m: A metropolitan region joins the core city and its surroundings into one economic area.

59133.q: Which geographer coined the term “Megalopolis” in 1961 for the band of cities between Boston and Washington?
59133.e: In his book “Megalopolis”, Jean Gottmann described the chain of cities growing together on the US East Coast. Later the short name “BosWash” was also used for it.
59133.m: Jean Gottmann called the band of cities on the US East Coast Megalopolis.

59134.q: Which polycentric metropolitan region in the Netherlands includes Amsterdam, Rotterdam, The Hague and Utrecht?
59134.e: The Randstad consists of several large cities without a single dominant core city. In its middle lies the largely undeveloped “Green Heart”.
59134.m: The Randstad is a metropolitan region with several equal centres.

59135.q: What is the most populous metropolitan region in Germany called?
59135.e: The Rhine-Ruhr metropolitan region, with cities such as Cologne, Düsseldorf, Dortmund and Essen, has about 10 million inhabitants. It is strongly polycentric.
59135.m: Rhine-Ruhr is Germany's most populous metropolitan region.

59136.q: Which French geographer described the densely populated belt from southern England to northern Italy in 1989, later called the “Blue Banana”?
59136.e: In a study, Roger Brunet showed that Europe's population and economy are concentrated in a curved band. Switzerland lies in this band.
59136.m: The Blue Banana is Europe's economic backbone.

59137.q: Which metropolitan region on Lake Geneva links the urban areas of Geneva and Lausanne?
59137.e: The Arc lémanique covers the areas around Geneva and Lausanne, with many international organisations and universities. Alongside Zurich and Basel, it counts as a metropolitan region of Switzerland.
59137.m: Geneva and Lausanne together form the Arc lémanique metropolitan region.

59138.q: Which feature characterises a monocentric metropolitan region?
59138.e: In a monocentric metropolitan region, jobs and traffic are focused on one core city, such as Paris. Polycentric regions such as Rhine-Ruhr, on the other hand, have several centres.
59138.m: A monocentric metropolitan region has only one large centre.

59139.q: Which figure is often used to define the extent of a metropolitan region?
a: The share of commuters to the core city
59139.e: Municipalities from which a certain share of workers commute to the core city are counted as part of the region. This way the boundary reflects functional links.
59139.m: Commuter flows show how far a metropolitan region reaches.

59140.q: Which metropolitan region in Germany is polycentric, meaning it has grown together from several large cities of about equal importance?
59140.e: In the Rhine-Ruhr region, cities such as Cologne, Düsseldorf, Dortmund and Essen lie close together, and none dominates alone. Munich, Hamburg and Berlin, by contrast, are clearly focused on one core city.
59140.m: Rhine-Ruhr is a metropolitan region with many centres.

59141.q: Which European capital is a classic example of a primate city because it towers far above all the other cities of its country?
59141.e: Almost a fifth of France's population lives in the Paris region, and Lyon and Marseille are much smaller. Berlin, Bern and Rome do not tower so much above the other cities of their countries.
59141.m: Paris is Europe's typical primate city.

59142.q: According to a common rule of thumb, when do we speak of a primate city?
a: When it is at least twice as large as the second largest city
When it is exactly the same size as the second largest city
When it has more than 100,000 inhabitants
When it is the oldest city in the country
59142.e: A primate city clearly towers above the other cities of a country in population, economy and politics. Twice the size of the second largest city is often given as a guideline.
59142.m: A primate city is much larger than all the other cities in its country.

59143.q: Which city is considered a particularly pronounced primate city in South-East Asia?
59143.e: The Bangkok urban area is many times larger than any other city in Thailand. Almost all the country's important functions are concentrated there.
59143.m: Bangkok towers far above all the other cities in Thailand.

59144.q: Which rule says that the second largest city of a country has about half as many inhabitants as the largest?
59144.e: Zipf's rank-size rule describes a balanced urban hierarchy: the city ranked n has about one nth of the inhabitants of the largest city. Primate cities differ clearly from this.
59144.m: According to the rank-size rule, city sizes decrease evenly.

59145.q: Which city is often given as an example of an oversized capital, a so-called “Wasserkopf” (water head), in Austria?
59145.e: Vienna has about two million inhabitants, while Graz, the second largest city, has only about 300,000. This imbalance goes back to Vienna's former role as the capital of a large empire.
59145.m: Vienna is an oversized capital for Austria.

59146.q: Which historical cause is given for many primate cities in former colonies?
a: Administration and trade being focused on one port
59146.e: Colonial powers often concentrated administration, ports and transport routes in a single place. This concentration continued after independence.
59146.m: Many primate cities arose because colonial administration was concentrated in one place.

59147.q: Which city in South America is a classic example of a primate city?
59147.e: About a third of Peru's population lives in the Lima region. The second largest city, Arequipa, is many times smaller.

59148.q: What consequence does a strong primate city often have for a country?
59148.e: Investment, jobs and educational institutions cluster in the primate city. Other regions fall behind, which further increases migration to the metropolis.
59148.m: Primate cities often widen the gap between centre and periphery.

59149.q: What is an urban system without a dominant city called, as seen in Switzerland with several medium-sized centres?
59149.e: In Switzerland, Zurich, Geneva, Basel, Bern and Lausanne share important functions. The federal state and federalism encourage this distribution.
59149.m: Switzerland has a polycentric urban system.

59150.q: Where does the name “favela” originally come from?
59150.e: At the end of the 19th century, soldiers from the Canudos War settled on a hill in Rio and named it after the favela plant. The name was later passed on to all similar settlements.
59150.m: Favelas are named after a plant from north-eastern Brazil.

59151.q: Which hill in Rio de Janeiro is considered the site of the first favela?
59151.e: The first favela arose at the end of the 19th century on the Morro da Providência near the port. At that time it was also called Morro da Favela.
59151.m: The first favela arose on the Morro da Providência.

59152.q: Which favela is considered the most populous in Rio de Janeiro?
59152.e: Rocinha lies on a steep slope between the districts of Gávea and São Conrado. The 2022 census counted about 72,000 inhabitants there, and unofficial estimates are higher.

59153.q: What are informal shanty towns called in French-speaking countries?
59153.e: The word comes from “bidon”, meaning a can or tin container, from which many huts used to be built. There were bidonvilles in Morocco and Algeria, for example, and until the 1970s also on the edge of Paris.
59153.m: In French-speaking countries, slums are called bidonvilles.

59154.q: What are informal settlements called in Peru?
59154.e: Since the 1950s, many barriadas have grown up on the edge of Lima, often on desert land. Today they are usually called “pueblos jóvenes”.
59154.m: In Peru, informal settlements are called barriadas.

59155.q: What are programmes called that improve favelas on site with roads, water and sewers instead of demolishing them?
59155.e: In slum upgrading, residents stay where they are and the infrastructure is improved. In Rio, for example, the “Favela-Bairro” programme followed this approach.
59155.m: Slum upgrading improves favelas without driving out the residents.

59156.q: What was the aim of the “Unidades de Polícia Pacificadora” (UPP) deployed in Rio from 2008?
a: To drive drug gangs out of favelas and station police there permanently
To sell the favelas to private companies
59156.e: The pacification police were meant to establish state control in favelas ruled by gangs. The programme was controversial and later lost its effect.
59156.m: The UPP were meant to bring state control back to Rio's favelas.

59157.q: What legal problem do many favela residents have?
a: They lack property titles for their land
59157.e: Favelas mostly arose by occupying land without permission. Without property titles, residents can hardly borrow against their houses and are at risk of eviction.
59157.m: Many favela residents have no official title to their land.

59158.q: Roughly how large is the area of Dharavi in Mumbai?
59158.e: Depending on how it is defined, Dharavi covers just over 2 square kilometres. An estimated several hundred thousand to a million people live there, giving an extreme density.
59158.m: Dharavi is small in area but huge in population.

59159.q: Why has Dharavi grown so much?
a: Many people moved from the countryside to Mumbai to look for work
The government deliberately settled civil servants there
It was a popular holiday area
59159.e: As Bombay grew, many people moved there from rural regions of India. Because they could not afford regular housing, they built simple shelters on the former swamp.
59159.m: Dharavi grew through migration from the countryside to the city.

59160.q: Which industry is Dharavi particularly known for?
59160.e: In thousands of small workshops, plastic, metal and other waste is sorted and recycled. Leather goods, textiles and pottery are also common.
59160.m: In Dharavi, waste is recycled in many small businesses.

59161.q: Why is Dharavi considered very economically active despite its poverty?
a: Thousands of small businesses make large turnovers there
The headquarters of India's central bank is there
59161.e: In Dharavi, potters, tanners, tailors and recycling businesses work in a very small space. The yearly turnover of this informal economy is estimated at hundreds of millions of dollars.
59161.m: Dharavi is a slum with a very active informal economy.

59162.q: Why is Dharavi's location so attractive for property investors?
a: It is central, near the Bandra-Kurla business district
It is right next to Delhi airport
It lies on a plateau with oil
It lies on the border with Pakistan
59162.e: Dharavi lies between two important suburban railway lines and near the modern Bandra-Kurla Complex. The land is therefore very valuable, which drives plans for redevelopment.
59162.m: Dharavi lies on very valuable land in the middle of Mumbai.

59163.q: Which feature film, which won the Oscar for Best Picture in 2009, was partly filmed in Dharavi?
59163.e: “Slumdog Millionaire” tells the story of a young man from the slums of Mumbai. The film made Dharavi known internationally and sparked debates about slum tourism.
59163.m: The film “Slumdog Millionaire” made Dharavi famous worldwide.

59164.q: Which Indian company won the contract in 2022 for the major project to redevelop Dharavi?
59164.e: The government of Maharashtra awarded the redevelopment project to the Adani Group. Critics fear that many residents and small businesses will be pushed out.
59164.m: The Adani Group is to redevelop Dharavi.

59165.q: Which term describes the mix of living and working in a very small space that is typical of Dharavi?
59165.e: In Dharavi, many rooms serve as a workshop by day and a place to sleep at night. This close link between living and business is one reason for the high economic activity.
59165.m: In Dharavi, living and working are closely intertwined.

59166.q: In which municipality in the canton of Aargau did the Shoppi open in 1970, one of the first large shopping centres in Switzerland on the edge of a city?
59166.e: The Shoppi in Spreitenbach opened in March 1970 just outside Zurich and was easy to reach by car. It stands for the shift of shopping from the city centre to the surrounding area.
59166.m: With the Shoppi Spreitenbach, shopping in Switzerland moved to the edge of the city.

59167.q: In van den Berg's model of urban development, which stage follows suburbanisation?
59167.e: The stage model describes the sequence urbanisation, suburbanisation, counter-urbanisation and reurbanisation. In counter-urbanisation, the whole urban area loses inhabitants.
59167.m: In the stage model, counter-urbanisation follows suburbanisation.

59168.q: Which American suburban settlement from the late 1940s is seen as the symbol of mass-built suburbs?
59168.e: The firm Levitt & Sons built thousands of almost identical detached houses on Long Island using mass production. Levittown became the model for post-war suburbanisation in the USA.
59168.m: Levittown is the classic example of an American suburb.

59169.q: Which development most strongly encouraged suburbanisation in the 20th century?
59169.e: With their own car, people could live far from their place of work. Cheap building land and the wish for a home of one's own strengthened the development.
59169.m: The car made living in the surrounding area possible for many people.

59170.q: What is the disorderly spread of built-up areas into the countryside, a common consequence of suburbanisation, called?
59170.e: Urban sprawl produces scattered buildings with high land use and a lot of traffic. In German it is called “Zersiedelung”.
59170.m: Urban sprawl eats up countryside and creates a lot of traffic.

59171.q: Which federal revision did Swiss voters approve in 2013 to slow urban sprawl?
a: Revision of the Spatial Planning Act
Revision of the Road Traffic Act
59171.e: The revised Spatial Planning Act requires building zones that are too large to be reduced and development to be concentrated inwards. It came into force in 2014.
59171.m: The 2013 Spatial Planning Act is meant to slow urban sprawl in Switzerland.

59172.q: What was the name of the federal popular initiative that called for building zones to be frozen and was rejected in 2019?
59172.e: The initiative by the Young Greens wanted to limit the total area of building zones. The people and the cantons clearly rejected it in February 2019.
59172.m: The Urban Sprawl Initiative was rejected in 2019.

59173.q: Which effect describes a core city whose centre loses inhabitants while the ring around it grows?
59173.e: As with a doughnut, a hole remains in the middle while the population concentrates around the edge. The effect is a typical consequence of strong suburbanisation.
59173.m: In the doughnut effect, the city centre empties and the outskirts grow.

59174.q: Which sociologist coined the term “gentrification” in London in 1964?
59174.e: Ruth Glass observed how middle-class households moved into working-class areas of London and pushed out the previous residents. She took the term from “gentry”, the English lower nobility.
59174.m: Ruth Glass coined the term gentrification in 1964.

59175.q: In the classic stage model of gentrification, which group is the first to move into a cheap area of old buildings?
a: Pioneers such as students and artists
59175.e: Pioneers look for cheap housing and make an area attractive with studios, bars and culture. They are followed by gentrifiers who can pay more.
59175.m: Gentrification usually begins with the pioneers.

59176.q: Which theory by Neil Smith explains gentrification by the difference between the current and the possible ground rent?
59176.e: When the rent actually earned is far below what is possible, investing in renovation pays off. Smith calls this gap the “rent gap”.
59176.m: According to rent gap theory, a large rent gap attracts investors.

59177.q: Which consequence of gentrification is criticised most often?
59177.e: After renovations, rents rise sharply so that previous residents can no longer afford their homes. They have to move to cheaper areas.
59177.m: Gentrification can push out long-standing residents.

59178.q: Which part of Berlin is a well-known example of gentrification after reunification?
59178.e: In GDR times, Prenzlauer Berg was an area of unrenovated old buildings. After 1990 it was extensively renovated and its population was largely replaced.
59178.m: Prenzlauer Berg is a textbook example of gentrification in Berlin.

59179.q: Which area of Zurich is often given as an example of gentrification after former industrial sites there were converted?
59179.e: In District 5, old factory and business sites were converted into flats, offices and cultural venues. Rents in the area rose markedly as a result.
59179.m: Zürich-West changed from an industrial area into a sought-after place to live.

59180.q: What is gentrification caused by short-term holiday lets in city centres called?
59180.e: When flats are permanently let to tourists, they are no longer available to local people. Cities such as Barcelona or Lisbon responded with restrictions.
59180.m: Touristification pushes out local people through holiday flats.

59181.q: Which instrument do German cities use to limit luxury renovations in certain areas?
59181.e: With a social preservation bylaw, often called Milieuschutz, building changes need approval. This is meant to protect the established population.
59181.m: Milieuschutz is meant to protect residents from being pushed out by luxury renovation.

59182.q: What is Lagos called in the Yoruba language?
59182.e: The Yoruba call the city Eko. The name Lagos, on the other hand, comes from Portuguese seafarers.
59182.m: In Yoruba, Lagos is called Eko.

59183.q: What is the new district of Lagos called that is being built on land reclaimed from the sea?
59183.e: Eko Atlantic is being built on sand dredged from the sea and is protected by a sea wall. The project is aimed mainly at wealthy residents and companies.
59183.m: Eko Atlantic is a new luxury district on reclaimed land.

59184.q: What are the yellow minibuses that provide a large part of public transport in Lagos called?
59184.e: Danfos are private minibuses that run on fixed routes without an exact timetable. They are part of the city's informal transport sector.
59184.m: In Lagos, many people travel in yellow danfo buses.

59185.q: Which film industry has its centre in Lagos?
59185.e: Nollywood is the Nigerian film industry and produces a great many films every year. Many production companies are based in Lagos.
59185.m: Lagos is the centre of Nollywood.

59186.q: On which island is the old trading centre of Lagos?
59186.e: Lagos Island was the historic core of the city, with ports and markets. Today it is connected to the mainland by bridges.
59186.m: The historic centre of Lagos is on Lagos Island.

59187.q: Because of its location on a lagoon and the coast, which natural hazard particularly threatens Lagos?
59187.e: Large parts of Lagos lie only a little above sea level. Heavy rain, blocked drains and coastal erosion often lead to flooding.
59187.m: Lagos is seriously at risk from floods and rising sea levels.

59188.q: Which railway line opened in 2023 as the first urban rail line in Lagos?
59188.e: The Blue Line of the Lagos Rail Mass Transit started running in 2023. It is meant to relieve the heavily congested road traffic.
59188.m: The Blue Line was Lagos's first urban rail line.

59189.q: Which colonial power made Lagos its colony in 1861?
59189.e: Great Britain annexed Lagos in 1861. Later the city became part of the colony of Nigeria, which became independent in 1960.
59189.m: Lagos became a British colony in 1861.

59190.q: Which city of over a million lies in the urban area between Tokyo and Yokohama?
59190.e: Kawasaki lies on the Tama River between Tokyo and Yokohama and has about 1.5 million inhabitants. The city is an important industrial location on the bay.
59190.m: Kawasaki joins Tokyo and Yokohama into one continuous urban area.

59191.q: What does Yokohama use former shipyard and port areas for today in the Minato Mirai 21 district?
a: As a modern business, residential and leisure district
As a nature reserve for migrating birds
As a base for the fishing fleet
59191.e: Minato Mirai 21 was built from the 1980s on the sites of old shipyards and reclaimed land. It was meant to strengthen Yokohama as a centre in its own right alongside Tokyo.
59191.m: Minato Mirai 21 is Yokohama's modern harbour district.

59192.q: After Tokyo, which is the second largest city in Japan by population?
59192.e: Yokohama has about 3.7 million inhabitants and lies south of Tokyo on the bay. Its port was opened to foreign trade in 1859.
59192.m: Yokohama is the second largest city in Japan.

59193.q: What are the railway staff in Tokyo called who push passengers into full trains at rush hour?
59193.e: The Japanese word “oshiya” means something like “pusher”. They show how heavily the commuter network of the Tokyo region is used.
59193.m: In Tokyo, oshiya help push commuters into overcrowded trains.

59194.q: Which earthquake destroyed large parts of Tokyo and Yokohama in 1923?
59194.e: More than 100,000 people died in the Great Kantō earthquake, many in the fires that followed. The rebuilding shaped Tokyo's town planning.
59194.m: The 1923 Kantō earthquake devastated Tokyo and Yokohama.

59195.q: What is the densely populated band of cities from Tokyo via Nagoya and Osaka to Fukuoka called?
59195.e: The Taiheiyō Belt, also called the Pacific Belt or Tōkaidō corridor, stretches about 1200 kilometres from Ibaraki Prefecture to Fukuoka. A large part of Japan's population lives in this band.
59195.m: The Taiheiyō Belt is Japan's great band of cities.

59196.q: How many special wards make up the core of Tokyo Prefecture?
59196.e: The 23 special wards, such as Shinjuku, Shibuya or Chiyoda, form the former city area of Tokyo. Each ward has its own administration.
59196.m: The core of Tokyo consists of 23 special wards.

59197.q: Which railway line opened in 1964 between Tokyo and Osaka as the world's first high-speed line?
59197.e: The Tōkaidō Shinkansen started running shortly before the 1964 Tokyo Olympics. It connects Japan's two largest urban areas.
59197.m: The first Shinkansen ran from Tokyo to Osaka in 1964.

59198.q: How has Tokyo gained new space for the port, industry and housing in Tokyo Bay over time?
a: Through land reclamation by filling in the bay
59198.e: Since the Edo period, artificial land has repeatedly been created in the bay, for example Odaiba. A large part of the shoreline today consists of reclaimed land.
59198.m: Tokyo has gained a lot of space by filling in parts of the bay.

59199.q: Which area does Shenzhen border to the south?
59199.e: Shenzhen lies directly north of Hong Kong. Being close to capital and know-how from Hong Kong was an important reason for choosing it as a special economic zone.

59200.q: Together with Guangzhou, Hong Kong and Macau, which large economic area does Shenzhen belong to?
59200.e: The Pearl River Delta, today also called the “Greater Bay Area”, is one of the largest industrial and urban areas in the world. Many electronic products are made here.
59200.m: Shenzhen lies in the Pearl River Delta.

59201.q: Roughly how many inhabitants did Shenzhen have in the 2020 Chinese census?
59201.e: The 2020 census gave Shenzhen just under 17.6 million inhabitants. In 1980 only a few hundred thousand people lived in the area.
59201.m: Shenzhen had about 17.5 million inhabitants in 2020.

59202.q: What is Shenzhen particularly famous for worldwide today?
59202.e: Many smartphones and components are developed and made in Shenzhen. Companies such as Huawei, Tencent and BYD are based here.
59202.m: Shenzhen is a centre of the electronics industry.

59203.q: What did Shenzhen achieve in public transport in 2017?
a: Its entire bus fleet ran on electricity
59203.e: Shenzhen was the first big city in the world to switch its entire fleet of over 16,000 city buses to electric power. Many taxis also run on electricity.
59203.m: In 2017 Shenzhen was the first big city to have only electric buses.

59204.q: Which technology company has its headquarters in Shenzhen?
59204.e: Huawei was founded in Shenzhen in 1987 and still has its headquarters there. Tencent and BYD also come from Shenzhen.
59204.m: Huawei has its headquarters in Shenzhen.

59205.q: What is the key feature of a smart city?
a: Using digital technology and data to manage city processes
Doing without any kind of technology
59205.e: A smart city uses sensors, networks and data analysis, for example for traffic, energy or waste. The aim is more efficiency, sustainability and quality of life.
59205.m: A smart city manages its processes with data and digital technology.

59206.q: Which city in South Korea was newly built as a smart city on reclaimed land from the 2000s?
59206.e: Songdo near Incheon was planned with networked infrastructure from the start. Critics say that despite the technology, the city does not feel very lively.
59206.m: Songdo is a smart city in South Korea planned from scratch.

59207.q: Which project near Abu Dhabi was meant to be built as a particularly climate-friendly planned city?
59207.e: From 2008, Masdar City was planned as a city with renewable energy and little car traffic. The original goals were scaled back several times.
59207.m: Masdar City is a planned eco-city near Abu Dhabi.

59208.q: Which city state launched the “Smart Nation” initiative in 2014?
59208.e: Singapore relies nationwide on sensors, digital government services and data-based traffic control. In rankings, the country is often seen as a leading smart city.
59208.m: Since 2014 Singapore has aimed to become a Smart Nation.

59209.q: Which smart city project in Toronto by a subsidiary of Alphabet was cancelled in 2020?
59209.e: Sidewalk Labs wanted to build a data-driven district on Toronto's waterfront. After criticism over data protection and because of the pandemic, the project was abandoned.
59209.m: The smart city project in Toronto failed partly over data protection.

59210.q: What is a digital copy of a city, with which plans can be tested virtually, called?
59210.e: A digital twin reproduces buildings, traffic and infrastructure in real time. Cities such as Zurich use 3D city models as a basis for this.
59210.m: A digital twin is a virtual copy of the city.

59211.q: What is an electricity grid called that intelligently matches generation and consumption using data?
59211.e: A smart grid connects power stations, storage and consumers through communication technology. This makes it easier to include fluctuating energy such as solar and wind.
59211.m: A smart grid controls the power grid with data.

59212.q: Which criticism of smart cities is mentioned most often?
a: Traffic lights with too little computing power
59212.e: Smart cities collect large amounts of data about residents' movements and behaviour. Critics warn of surveillance and the power of private technology companies.
59212.m: Smart cities raise important questions about data protection.

59213.q: Which journalist made the term “edge city” well known with a book in 1991?
59213.e: In “Edge City: Life on the New Frontier”, Joel Garreau described new centres on the edge of large American cities. He set out fixed criteria for them.
59213.m: Joel Garreau coined the term edge city.

59214.q: Which criterion did Joel Garreau give for an edge city?
59214.e: An edge city is a place people commute to for work in the morning. That is why there are more jobs there than homes.
59214.m: An edge city has more jobs than bedrooms.

59215.q: How does an edge city differ from a pure dormitory town?
a: It offers many jobs, offices and shopping centres
It has a medieval old town
It always lies right by the sea
59215.e: Commuters return to a dormitory town only to live there. An edge city, by contrast, is itself a destination for commuters, with large office spaces and shopping centres.
59215.m: An edge city is a centre for work and shopping on the edge of a city.

59216.q: Which place near Washington D.C. is considered a textbook example of an edge city?
59216.e: Tysons Corner in Virginia grew up at motorway junctions out of shopping centres and office towers. For a long time there were hardly any homes there and no railway connection of its own.
59216.m: Tysons Corner is a classic example of an edge city.

59217.q: Where do edge cities typically develop?
a: At motorway junctions in the area around large cities
59217.e: Edge cities grow where motorways offer good access and cheap building land. They are strongly geared to the car.
59217.m: Edge cities usually lie at motorway junctions on the edge of cities.

59218.q: Which stage of development after suburbanisation is linked to the rise of edge cities?
59218.e: In post-suburbanisation, independent centres with jobs, shops and leisure arise in the surrounding area. The surrounding area is then no longer just a place to live.
59218.m: Edge cities are a feature of post-suburbanisation.

59219.q: Which problem are edge cities often accused of?
a: They are strongly geared to the car
They have too many pedestrian zones
They are too far from motorways
They consist only of historic buildings
59219.e: Edge cities mostly grew up at motorway junctions with large car parks. Without a car, many offices and shopping centres are hard to reach, which increases traffic and land use.

59220.q: Which area north of Zurich is often given as a Swiss example of a development similar to an edge city?
59220.e: In the Glattal between Zurich and the airport, office centres, shopping centres and new residential areas have grown up. Since 2010 the Glattalbahn tram has linked these centres all the way through.
59220.m: The Glattal has developed into a new centre just outside Zurich.

59221.q: Which sociologist published the concentric ring model of a city in 1925?
59221.e: Ernest W. Burgess presented the ring model in 1925 in the volume “The City”, which he edited with Robert E. Park. It describes the city as a series of concentric zones around a centre.
59221.m: In 1925 Burgess described the city as a series of rings.

59222.q: Which city served as Burgess's model for his ring model?
59222.e: Burgess did research at the University of Chicago and derived his model from the development of Chicago. Because of Lake Michigan, the zones there actually form semicircles.
59222.m: The ring model was based on the example of Chicago.

59223.q: In the ring model, which zone lies directly around the central business district?
59223.e: Directly next to the centre is the zone in transition, with businesses, old buildings and cheap housing. Newly arrived immigrants often lived here.
59223.m: In Burgess's model, the zone in transition lies just beyond the centre.

59224.q: Which zone forms the outermost ring in Burgess's ring model?
59224.e: The outermost ring is the commuter zone, with suburbs of well-off households. Its residents travel to work in the centre every day.
59224.m: In the ring model, the commuter zone lies furthest out.

59225.q: From which science did Burgess take the terms invasion and succession?
