59225.e: Burgess and his colleagues applied terms from plant and animal ecology to the city. Groups move into an area (invasion) and push out the previous residents (succession).
59225.m: Burgess explained urban change with terms from ecology.

59226.q: In the ring model, how does the social status of residents change from the centre outwards?
a: It is highest in the middle
59226.e: According to Burgess, poorer groups live near the centre and well-off households further out. As their income grows, families move to outer rings.
59226.m: In the ring model, the wealthy tend to live on the edge of the city.

59227.q: How many zones does Burgess's classic ring model have?
59227.e: Burgess distinguished five zones, from the business centre in the core to the outermost residential ring.
59227.m: The ring model consists of five concentric zones.

59228.q: Which criticism is often made of the ring model?
a: It overlooks transport routes and terrain
It only applies to port cities
59228.e: The model assumes a uniform flat surface and takes no account of transport routes, rivers or hills. It also mainly fits North American industrial cities of the 1920s.
59228.m: The ring model simplifies a lot because it ignores terrain and transport routes.

59229.q: Together with Robert E. Park, which school of research did Burgess belong to?
59229.e: Park and Burgess shaped the Chicago School of sociology, which used the city as a field of research. This gave rise to socio-ecological urban research.
59229.m: Burgess and Park belonged to the Chicago School of sociology.

59230.q: In the ring model, which force drives the city's growth outwards?
a: Laws made by the city government
59230.e: According to Burgess, immigration creates pressure on the inner zones. As a result, each zone expands into the next, rather like waves.
59230.m: In the ring model, immigration pushes the zones outwards.

59231.q: Who developed the sector model of the city in 1939?
59231.e: The economist Homer Hoyt published the model in 1939 after studying rents in US cities. At the time he was working for the federal housing agency.
59231.m: Homer Hoyt presented the sector model in 1939.

59232.q: What shape do the zones have in the sector model?
59232.e: In the sector model, wedge-shaped sectors reach from the centre outwards, like slices of a cake. Concentric rings belong to the older ring model.
59232.m: In the sector model, the city looks like a cake cut into slices.

59233.q: Along which structures are Hoyt's sectors mainly arranged?
59233.e: Hoyt observed that uses such as industry or housing spread out from the centre in wedges along roads, railway lines and rivers.
59233.m: In the sector model, uses grow along transport routes.

59234.q: Which data did Hoyt mainly analyse for his model?
59234.e: Hoyt mapped the average rents per block in many US cities. Areas of high rent showed up in the shape of sectors.
59234.m: Hoyt derived the sector model from rents.

59235.q: In the sector model, where does the upper-class sector typically lie?
a: Along attractive routes, often on higher ground
59235.e: Wealthy households prefer routes with good transport links, nice views or a location away from industry. Their sector expands outwards in this direction.
59235.m: In the sector model, the upper class lives along attractive routes.

59236.q: Which older model did Hoyt combine with his sector idea?
59236.e: Hoyt built on Burgess's ring model, which divides the city into concentric rings. He added wedges that grow outwards along transport routes.
59236.m: The sector model extends the ring model with wedges along transport routes.

59237.q: In the sector model, next to which sector does the working-class residential area typically lie?
59237.e: Working-class housing lies near factories and railway lines so that journeys to work are short. The upper class avoids this direction because of noise and fumes.
59237.m: In the sector model, working-class areas border on industry.

59238.q: In the sector model, in which direction does a high-rent residential area grow?
a: It continues outwards in the same sector
It jumps randomly into other sectors
It forms a ring around the city
59238.e: According to Hoyt, sectors keep their character as the city grows. New upmarket areas arise on the outer side of the existing upper-class sector.
59238.m: According to Hoyt, upmarket sectors keep growing outwards in their direction.

59239.q: Which weakness is the sector model often accused of?
a: It has only one single centre
It does not describe residential areas
59239.e: Like the ring model, the sector model assumes only one business centre. Modern cities, however, often have several centres.
59239.m: The sector model neglects cities with several centres.

59240.q: In the sector model, which use lies at the centre from which all sectors start?
59240.e: All sectors begin at the central business district. From there they spread out in wedges along the transport routes.
59240.m: In the sector model, all wedges start from the business centre.

59241.q: Which two geographers published the multiple nuclei model in 1945?
59241.e: Chauncy D. Harris and Edward L. Ullman presented the model in 1945 in the essay “The Nature of Cities”. It adds to the older models with only one centre.
59241.m: Harris and Ullman developed the multiple nuclei model in 1945.

59242.q: What is the central idea of the multiple nuclei model?
a: A city grows around several nuclei
A city is shaped like a cross
59242.e: According to Harris and Ullman, uses develop around several nuclei, such as business centres, industrial areas or universities. Over time these nuclei grow together.
59242.m: The multiple nuclei model describes the city with several centres.

59243.q: According to the multiple nuclei model, why are some uses far apart?
a: All nuclei are the same size
59243.e: Harris and Ullman gave as a reason that opposing uses avoid each other, for example heavy industry and upmarket residential areas. Similar uses, on the other hand, attract each other.
59243.m: In the multiple nuclei model, incompatible uses avoid each other.

59244.q: Which example best fits a secondary nucleus in the multiple nuclei model?
a: A shopping centre on the edge of town
59244.e: A shopping centre on the edge of town attracts customers, other shops and traffic. In this way it becomes a nucleus of its own alongside the old city centre.
59244.m: Shopping centres on the edge of town can form new nuclei of a city.

59245.q: Why does the multiple nuclei model fit car-friendly cities well?
a: The car makes many locations reachable
59245.e: With a car, places away from the old centre are also easy to reach. As a result, extra business and industrial nuclei grow up along main roads out of town.
59245.m: The car encourages cities with several nuclei.

59246.q: In the multiple nuclei model, which factor causes similar businesses to be located close together?
a: They have to pay the same rent
59246.e: Similar businesses share customers, suppliers and skilled workers. These advantages of being close together are called agglomeration advantages.
59246.m: Similar businesses cluster because they benefit from each other.

59247.q: Which term describes large office centres on the edge of a city that grow as new nuclei?
59247.e: The journalist Joel Garreau coined the term edge city in 1991. Such centres usually develop at motorway junctions on the edge of large US cities.
59247.m: Edge cities are new office centres on the edge of large cities.

59248.q: Which feature distinguishes the multiple nuclei model from the older models?
a: It does not need a regular pattern
It only applies to port cities
59248.e: The multiple nuclei model does not set a fixed geometric shape. The location of the nuclei depends on the history, terrain and transport of each city.
59248.m: The multiple nuclei model has no rigid geometric shape.

59249.q: In the multiple nuclei model, which use usually lies far from the business centre?
59249.e: Heavy industry needs a lot of space, a rail connection and cheap land. That is why in the model it lies away from the central business district.
59249.m: In the multiple nuclei model, heavy industry usually lies far from the centre.

59250.q: How many reasons for the formation of nuclei did Harris and Ullman give?
59250.e: They gave four reasons: special location needs, attraction of similar uses, repulsion of opposing uses and different ability to pay for land.
59250.m: Harris and Ullman explained the formation of nuclei with four reasons.

59251.q: What is the traditional old town of an oriental city in North Africa called?
59251.e: The medina is the old town, often walled, with narrow alleys, mosques and souks. The Arabic word simply means city.
59251.m: The old town of a North African city is called the medina.

59252.q: Which building traditionally forms the centre of an oriental old town?
59252.e: The great Friday mosque usually lies in the centre of the medina. The market alleys of the souk are grouped around it.
59252.m: The Friday mosque stands at the heart of the oriental old town.

59253.q: What is the market area of an Arab old town called?
59253.e: The souk is a maze of market alleys where traders and craftspeople have their shops. In Persia and Turkey it is called a bazaar.
59253.m: The market of the Arab old town is called the souk.

59254.q: Where in the souk do traders of valuable goods such as gold or books typically have their shops?
59254.e: The layout of the souk follows a ranking: fine, clean goods are near the mosque. Noisy or smelly trades are further out.
59254.m: In the souk, valuable goods are sold near the main mosque.

59255.q: Why are tanneries in a medina usually on the edge of the old town?
a: Because of the high rents in the centre
59255.e: Tanneries process animal hides with strong-smelling substances. That is why they lie far from the mosque and the fine goods, on the edge of the old town.
59255.m: Smelly trades are on the edge of the medina.

59256.q: What is the purpose of the many dead-end alleys in the residential areas of a medina?
59256.e: Dead-end alleys keep strangers away from the houses and so protect families' privacy. Life takes place in the inward-facing courtyard house.
59256.m: Dead-end alleys protect families' privacy in the medina.

59257.q: Which type of house is typical of the residential areas of an oriental old town?
59257.e: The rooms open onto an inner courtyard, and there are hardly any windows facing the alley. This protects family life and privacy, and the courtyard gives shade.
59257.m: Oriental houses open onto the inner courtyard rather than the alley.

59258.q: Which Moroccan medina is considered one of the largest car-free urban areas in the world?
59258.e: The old town of Fès el-Bali has thousands of narrow alleys in which loads are carried by donkeys and carts. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1981.
59258.m: Fès el-Bali is a huge car-free old town in Morocco.

59259.q: What is the fortified citadel called that lies on the edge of the medina in many North African cities?
59259.e: The kasbah was the seat of the ruler and his troops and often lies on high ground on the edge of the old town. A well-known example is the Kasbah of the Udayas in Rabat.
59259.m: The kasbah is the fortress on the edge of the medina.

59260.q: What is the historic Jewish quarter in Moroccan cities called?
59260.e: The mellah was often near the ruler's palace, which offered its residents protection. The mellah of Fès was founded in the 15th century.
59260.m: The Jewish quarter of Moroccan cities is called the mellah.

59261.q: Which square forms the centre of a Spanish colonial city in Latin America?
59261.e: The cathedral, town hall and governor's residence stood around the Plaza Mayor. In Mexico the main square is often called the Zócalo.
59261.m: The Plaza Mayor is the centre of the Spanish colonial city.

59262.q: Which body of laws set the layout of Spanish colonial cities in 1573?
a: Leyes de Indias (Laws of the Indies)
59262.e: In 1573 King Philip II issued rules for founding cities in the Americas, which became part of the Laws of the Indies. They required a central square and a grid of streets at right angles.
59262.m: The Laws of the Indies set the grid plan of the colonial cities.

59263.q: How was the social structure of the colonial city arranged from the centre outwards?
a: All classes lived mixed on the edge
The upper class lived outside the city
59263.e: In colonial times the upper class lived right on the plaza. The further from the centre, the poorer the residents, the opposite of North American cities.
59263.m: In the colonial city, the rich lived on the main square.

59264.q: Which German geographers developed a well-known model of the Latin American city in 1981?
59264.e: Jürgen Bahr and Günter Mertins described the city with ring-shaped, sector-shaped and cell-like elements. Their model is often used in geography lessons in German-speaking countries.
59264.m: Bahr and Mertins created a model of the Latin American city in 1981.

59265.q: In Griffin and Ford's model, what does the term “spine” mean?
a: A business axis lined with upper-class areas
A wall around the old town
59265.e: The spine is an axis that starts from the centre and is lined with shops and upper-class residential areas. The model dates from 1980.
59265.m: The spine is the grand axis of the Latin American city.

59266.q: What are informal settlements called in Argentina?
59266.e: In Argentina such settlements are called villas miseria, or villas for short. The name means something like settlements of misery.
59266.m: In Argentina, informal settlements are called villas miseria.

59267.q: Which feature shows the strong segregation in many large Latin American cities particularly clearly?
a: Favelas border directly on rich districts
All classes live in tower blocks
59267.e: In cities such as Rio de Janeiro, informal settlements on hillsides often lie right next to wealthy areas. Rich and poor are close in space but strongly separated socially.
59267.m: In Latin American cities, rich and poor often live right next to each other.

59268.q: Since the middle of the 20th century, where have many informal settlements in Latin American cities developed?
a: On the edge of the city and on steep slopes
59268.e: Strong rural exodus led to informal settlements on free land on the edge of the city and on slopes. These areas were not in demand and often had no services.
59268.m: Informal settlements often developed on the edge of the city and on steep slopes.

59269.q: Which process particularly drove the rapid growth of large Latin American cities in the 20th century?
59269.e: Many people moved from the countryside to the cities in search of work. As a result, cities such as Mexico City, São Paulo or Lima grew very quickly.
59269.m: Rural exodus made Latin America's big cities grow rapidly.

59270.q: In Peru, what are informal settlements on the edge of Lima called?
59270.e: Pueblos jóvenes literally means young villages. The term was introduced in Peru for formerly informal settlements that were gradually improved.
59270.m: In Lima, informal settlements are called pueblos jóvenes.

59271.q: Which Greek town planner gave his name to the right-angled street layout?
59271.e: Hippodamus of Miletus lived in the 5th century BC and planned Piraeus, among other places. The right-angled grid is therefore also called the Hippodamian plan.
59271.m: The right-angled street grid is called the Hippodamian plan after Hippodamus.

59272.q: Which famous street crosses Manhattan's right-angled street grid diagonally because it is older than the grid?
59272.e: The 1811 plan divided Manhattan into a grid of avenues and numbered streets. Broadway follows an old path and therefore runs at an angle to it.
59272.m: Broadway is older than Manhattan's street grid.

59273.q: Why do fields and roads in the Midwest of the USA look like a chessboard from the air?
a: From 1785 the land was surveyed into a state square grid
The fields follow the contour lines
Rivers divided the land at right angles
The Native Americans laid out the grid
59273.e: The Land Ordinance of 1785 divided the land west of the founding states into squares of 6 by 6 miles. This grid still shapes fields, roads and towns today.
59273.m: A state square grid shapes the Midwest of the USA.

59274.q: Roughly how long is a mile, the basic unit of the American land survey grid?
59274.e: A statute mile measures 1609 metres. The US grid divides the land into square miles, called sections.
59274.m: A mile is about 1.6 kilometres long.

59275.q: Which Swiss watchmaking town is known for its right-angled layout and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
59275.e: After a fire in 1794, La Chaux-de-Fonds was rebuilt according to a grid plan. Together with Le Locle, it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2009.
59275.m: La Chaux-de-Fonds is a watchmaking town with a chessboard layout.

59276.q: Which German city is called the “city of squares” because of its grid?
59276.e: Mannheim's city centre is divided into squares with letters and numbers, for example “P 7”. That is why addresses often give a square instead of a street name.
59276.m: Mannheim's city centre is divided into numbered squares.

59277.q: What were the two main streets of a Roman camp with a grid layout called?
59277.e: The cardo usually ran from north to south and the decumanus from east to west. The centre of the camp lay where they crossed.
59277.m: The cardo and decumanus crossed in the Roman camp.

59278.q: Which advantage made the chessboard layout popular when North America was settled?
a: Land was easy to survey and sell
It was required by the king
59278.e: Rectangular plots are easy to survey, number and sell. This made it easier to take over land quickly and speculate with it.
59278.m: The grid made it easier to survey and sell land.

59279.q: Which city did William Penn plan in 1682 with a grid and five squares?
59279.e: William Penn had Philadelphia laid out at right angles between the Delaware and Schuylkill rivers. Five public squares broke up the grid.
59279.m: Philadelphia was planned as a grid city in 1682.

59280.q: Which phenomenon in Manhattan is called “Manhattanhenge”?
a: The sun sets exactly in line with the streets
A stone circle in Central Park
A wall of fog between skyscrapers
59280.e: Because the street grid is turned away from north, on a few days in May and July the sun lines up exactly with the cross streets. The name plays on Stonehenge.
59280.m: Manhattanhenge shows the sun exactly in line with the streets.

59281.q: What does the abbreviation CBD stand for in urban geography?
59281.e: The Central Business District is the central business area of a city. Offices, banks, shops and administration are concentrated there.
59281.m: The CBD is the central business district of a city.

59282.q: Why are land prices highest in the CBD?
a: It is the easiest place to reach
It has the most fertile soil
It always lies by the sea
59282.e: Transport routes meet in the centre, so customers and workers can get there easily. Businesses compete for this location and drive prices up.
59282.m: Being easy to reach makes land in the CBD expensive.

59283.q: Which model explains which use pays the most for land near the centre?
59283.e: William Alonso's bid rent model shows that retail and services can pay the highest rents in the centre. Housing and farming lie further out.
59283.m: The bid rent model explains the order of land uses by land price.

59284.q: How do the daytime and night-time populations of the CBD compare?
a: Many more people by day than at night
Many more people at night than by day
Both are about the same size
The CBD is almost empty by day
59284.e: Many people commute to work in the CBD but live elsewhere. That is why the daytime population is much larger than the night-time population.
59284.m: By day, many people work in the CBD who do not live there.

59285.q: What is the process called in which homes in the centre are pushed out by offices and shops?
59285.e: In CBD formation, services that can pay more push housing out of the city centre. As a result, the number of people living in the centre falls.
59285.m: CBD formation pushes homes out of the city centre.

59286.q: What is Chicago's CBD called, named after an elevated railway loop?
59286.e: The elevated railway runs round Chicago's business centre in a loop. That is why the CBD is called The Loop.
59286.m: Chicago's business centre is called The Loop.

59287.q: Which economic sector shapes a city's Central Business District (CBD)?
59287.e: Banks, insurance companies, offices, retail and administration are concentrated in the CBD. These are services, in other words the tertiary sector. Industry and agriculture can hardly pay the high land prices.
59287.m: The CBD is shaped by services.

59288.q: Which Paris office centre was built as a new business district outside the historic city centre?
59288.e: La Défense lies just west of the Paris city boundary and is one of the largest office centres in Europe. It keeps tower blocks out of the historic city centre.
59288.m: La Défense is the modern office centre on the edge of Paris.

59289.q: Why are buildings in the CBD especially tall?
a: Expensive land is used better that way
Tower blocks are cheaper than low buildings
It is required by law everywhere
The ground there is particularly soft
59289.e: When land is very expensive, it pays to build many storeys on the same area. That is why most tower blocks are built in the CBD.
59289.m: Expensive land leads to tower blocks in the CBD.

59290.q: What is the point with the highest land values within the CBD called?
59290.e: The Peak Land Value Intersection is usually a crossroads with a great many passers-by. From there, land values fall in all directions.
59290.m: The most expensive point in the CBD is usually at a busy crossroads.

a: A closed residential area with controlled access
A housing cooperative without a fence
An industrial area by the harbour
59291.e: Gated communities are surrounded by walls or fences and have guarded entrances. Roads and facilities are private and only open to residents and guests.
59291.m: Gated communities are fenced residential areas with controlled access.

59292.q: What is the aim of town planners to have people with different incomes living together in one area called?
59292.e: Social mixing is the opposite of the isolation of gated communities. Segregation means spatial separation, and gentrification means poorer residents being pushed out by richer ones.
59292.m: Social mixing is the opposite model to gated communities.

59293.q: Which large closed residential development grew up near São Paulo from the 1970s?
59293.e: Alphaville lies west of São Paulo and includes several guarded residential areas as well as office and business centres. It is a well-known example of gated communities in Brazil.
59293.m: Alphaville is a well-known gated community near São Paulo.

59294.q: In urban geography, which spatial consequence is often attributed to gated communities?
59294.e: Gated communities separate wealthy households spatially from the rest of the population. This increases social segregation and the fragmentation of the city.
59294.m: Gated communities increase the separation of social groups.

59295.q: Which type of gated community mainly offers leisure facilities such as golf courses?
59295.e: Lifestyle communities are geared to leisure, for example with a golf course or offers for older people. Prestige communities, on the other hand, stress social status.
59295.m: Lifestyle communities attract people with leisure facilities such as golf courses.

59296.q: What are closed residential developments called in Brazil in Portuguese?
59296.e: Condomínio fechado means closed residential development. In Argentina, on the other hand, they are called barrios cerrados in Spanish.
59296.m: In Brazil, gated communities are called condomínios fechados.

59297.q: Which main motive do residents of gated communities in Latin America and South Africa mention particularly often?
59297.e: In cities with high crime, wealthy households seek protection behind walls and security guards. Prestige and lifestyle also play a role.
59297.m: The wish for safety encourages gated communities.

59298.q: Which large Argentine development on the Río Luján is considered one of the largest private urban settlements near Buenos Aires?
59298.e: Nordelta lies in the north of the Buenos Aires metropolitan region and consists of many guarded residential districts with lakes. It is a private planned town for the middle and upper classes.
59298.m: Nordelta is a large private settlement near Buenos Aires.

59299.q: In a gated community, who is usually responsible for roads, security and green spaces?
59299.e: Owners pay fees to a private management company that organises security and maintenance. In this way public tasks are privatised.
59299.m: In gated communities, private management takes over public tasks.

59300.q: Which country, with gated communities in cities such as Johannesburg, is an example outside the Americas?
59300.e: In South Africa, many guarded residential developments, known as security estates, were built after the end of apartheid. One reason is the high crime rate.
59300.m: South Africa also has many guarded residential developments.

59301.q: When was Brasília inaugurated as Brazil's new capital?
59301.e: Brasília was inaugurated on 21 April 1960. Building it took only about four years.

59302.q: Which president pushed ahead with building Brasília?
59302.e: Juscelino Kubitschek promised “50 years of progress in 5”. Brasília was the centrepiece of his development programme.

59303.q: Who designed the city plan of Brasília, the Plano Piloto?
59303.e: The town planner Lúcio Costa won the competition for the Plano Piloto in 1957. The buildings, on the other hand, were designed by another architect.
59303.m: Lúcio Costa designed the city plan of Brasília.

59304.q: Which architect designed the cathedral and the Congress building of Brasília?
59304.e: Oscar Niemeyer created the striking, curved concrete buildings. They include the cathedral and the National Congress with its two bowls.
59304.m: Oscar Niemeyer designed the buildings of Brasília.

59305.q: With which shape is the layout of the Plano Piloto often compared?
59305.e: Two crossing axes give the plan the shape of an aeroplane or bird. The Monumental Axis forms the body, and the curved residential axis forms the wings.
59305.m: The plan of Brasília looks like an aeroplane.

59306.q: Which city was Brazil's capital before Brasília?
59306.e: Rio de Janeiro was the capital from 1763 to 1960. With Brasília, the seat of government was moved inland.
59306.m: Before Brasília, Rio de Janeiro was the capital.

59307.q: What are the large residential units along the wings of Brasília called?
59307.e: Superquadras are blocks of flats with green spaces, schools and shops. They were meant to bring people of different classes together.
59307.m: Brasília's residential areas are called superquadras.

59308.q: What aim did Brazil have in moving the capital inland?
59308.e: A capital in the centre was meant to encourage the development of the thinly populated interior. Until then most people lived near the Atlantic coast.
59308.m: Brasília was meant to open up Brazil's interior.

59309.q: What are the settlements outside the Plano Piloto called, where many construction workers and poorer people live?
59309.e: The Plano Piloto offered too little cheap housing, so satellite towns such as Taguatinga or Ceilândia grew up. Today most of the Federal District's population lives there.
59309.m: Many people in Brasília live in satellite towns.

59310.q: Since when has Brasília been a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
59310.e: UNESCO added Brasília to the World Heritage List in 1987. The city is honoured as an outstanding example of 20th-century modern town planning and architecture.
59310.m: Brasília has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.

59311.q: Which ruling family governs the Emirate of Dubai?
59311.e: The Al Maktoum family has ruled Dubai since 1833. The Al Nahyan rule Abu Dhabi, the Al Saud Saudi Arabia and the Al Thani Qatar.
59311.m: Dubai is ruled by the Al Maktoum family.

59312.q: What is the artificial palm-shaped island off Dubai called?
59312.e: Palm Jumeirah was built from 2001 out of dredged sand. It holds villas, hotels and flats.
59312.m: Palm Jumeirah is Dubai's artificial palm island.

59313.q: On which inlet does the historic core of Dubai, with Deira and Bur Dubai, lie?
59313.e: Dubai Creek separates the old districts of Deira and Bur Dubai. This used to be the harbour for pearl divers and traders.
59313.m: Dubai Creek is the historic heart of Dubai.

59314.q: In which year was oil found off Dubai?
59314.e: The offshore Fateh oil field was discovered in 1966, and production began in 1969. The revenue financed the expansion of the city.
59314.m: Oil was discovered off Dubai in 1966.

59315.q: Why does Dubai rely heavily on trade, tourism and finance?
a: Its oil reserves are relatively small
Dubai is not allowed to sell oil
59315.e: Compared with Abu Dhabi, Dubai has only small oil reserves. That is why the emirate diversified its economy early on.
59315.m: Dubai diversified its economy because of its small oil reserves.

59316.q: What is the large port with a free trade zone in the south of Dubai called?
59316.e: Jebel Ali is one of the largest artificial ports in the world. Since 1985 the neighbouring free trade zone has attracted international companies.
59316.m: Jebel Ali is Dubai's large port with a free trade zone.

59317.q: Roughly what share of Dubai's population are foreign workers and immigrants?
59317.e: The vast majority of Dubai's inhabitants do not have a passport of the United Arab Emirates. Many come from India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and the Philippines.
59317.m: About nine in ten of Dubai's inhabitants are immigrants.

59318.q: Since which year has Dubai been part of the United Arab Emirates?
59318.e: After the end of the British protectorate, Dubai, Abu Dhabi and other emirates joined together in December 1971 to form the United Arab Emirates.
59318.m: Dubai has been part of the United Arab Emirates since 1971.

59319.q: Which means of transport did Dubai open in 2009 as a driverless rail system?
59319.e: The Dubai Metro started running in 2009 and operates automatically without drivers. Among other things, it connects the airport with Sheikh Zayed Road.
59319.m: The Dubai Metro has run without drivers since 2009.

59320.q: Which traditional building feature cooled the houses in the old Al Fahidi district?
59320.e: Wind towers, called barjeel in Arabic, catch the wind and direct it into the house. This creates cooling without electricity.
59320.m: Wind towers used to cool the houses in Dubai.

59321.q: Which country did the economist Jean Fourastié, to whom the three-sector hypothesis goes back, come from?
59321.e: Jean Fourastié (1907 to 1990) was a French economist. He made the model of the three economic sectors well known with his book of 1949.
59321.m: The three-sector hypothesis comes from the Frenchman Jean Fourastié.

59322.q: Which sector did Fourastié see as the “great hope” for employment and prosperity?
59322.e: In his 1949 book, Fourastié expected services to take on the workers no longer needed in agriculture and industry because of machines.
59322.m: Fourastié called the service sector the great hope of the 20th century.

59323.q: In the three-sector model, which branches of the economy belong to the primary sector?
59323.e: The primary sector covers primary production, meaning obtaining goods directly from nature.
59323.m: The primary sector obtains goods directly from nature.

59324.q: In Swiss statistics, which sector is construction assigned to?
59324.e: Construction turns materials into new goods and therefore belongs, like industry and trades, to the second sector.
59324.m: Industry, trades and construction form the secondary sector.

59325.q: How did Fourastié explain that the tertiary sector takes on the most workers in the long run?
a: Most goods are exported from there
59325.e: In agriculture and industry, productivity rises sharply thanks to machines, and fewer workers are needed. Many services can hardly be rationalised and take on the workers who are freed up.
59325.m: According to Fourastié, most jobs arise where machines can hardly replace work.

59326.q: According to the three-sector hypothesis, in which order do economies develop?
59326.e: First agriculture dominates, then industry and finally the service sector.
59326.m: The agricultural society is followed by the industrial and the service society.

59327.q: What is the shift of employment towards the service sector called?
59327.e: The term comes from the tertiary sector. It describes the growing share of services in employment and value added.
59327.m: Tertiarisation means the growth of the service sector.

59328.q: According to the three-sector hypothesis, which sector does a bank belong to?
59328.e: Banks do not make goods, they offer services. That is why, like retail, insurance and tourism, they belong to the tertiary sector.
59328.m: Banks belong to the service sector.

59329.q: Roughly what share of workers in Switzerland are employed in the primary sector (as of the 2020s)?
59329.e: According to figures from the Federal Statistical Office, only a few percent of workers are still employed in agriculture and forestry. Most work in the service sector.
59329.m: In Switzerland, only a small share of people work in the primary sector.

a: The decline in industry's share of the economy
59330.e: In deindustrialisation, employment and value added in the secondary sector fall, for example through automation or moving production abroad.
59330.m: Deindustrialisation means that industry is losing importance.

59331.q: In the extended division of sectors, what does the quaternary sector cover?
59331.e: The quaternary sector is separated out from the tertiary sector. It covers activities whose most important raw material is knowledge and information.
59331.m: In the quaternary sector, knowledge is the most important raw material.

59332.q: Which activity is typically assigned to the quaternary sector?
59332.e: The quaternary sector is part of the extended division of the economy. It covers activities whose most important raw material is knowledge and information.
59332.m: Software development is a typical activity of the quaternary sector.

59333.q: From which sector was the quaternary sector separated out?
59333.e: Because the service sector became very large and varied, the knowledge-intensive services were separated off as a sector of their own.
59333.m: The quaternary sector is part of what used to be services.

59334.q: Which location factor is usually particularly important for companies in the quaternary sector?
a: Being close to raw material deposits
59334.e: Knowledge-intensive firms need well-trained specialists. That is why they like to locate near universities and in big cities.
59334.m: Quaternary companies mainly look for well-trained skilled workers.

59335.q: With which concept of society is the growth of the quaternary sector often linked?
59335.e: In the knowledge society, knowledge becomes the most important resource for creating value. This shows in the growing information sector.
59335.m: The quaternary sector shapes the knowledge society.

59336.q: Which name is sometimes used for a fifth sector of top decision-makers in politics, business and science?
59336.e: Some models divide the quaternary sector further. The quinary sector is then made up of top positions in which important decisions are taken.
59336.m: The quinary sector covers the top decision-makers.

59337.q: Which Swiss institution is an example of the quaternary sector?
a: A research institute of ETH Zurich
A cheese dairy in the Emmental
59337.e: Research creates new knowledge and is therefore counted as part of the quaternary sector. The gravel pit, sawmill and cheese dairy belong to other sectors.
59337.m: Research at universities belongs to the quaternary sector.

59338.q: Which development has made the quaternary sector grow especially strongly since the 1990s?
59338.e: Computers, the internet and data processing created many new jobs around information and communication.
59338.m: Digitalisation made the information sector grow strongly.

59339.q: Why is it disputed where the quaternary sector ends and the tertiary sector begins?
a: Almost all services use information today
The quaternary sector employs no one
It can only be measured in Asia
59339.e: Banks, retail and administration also work heavily with data. That is why it is hard to say where a simple service ends and knowledge work begins.
59339.m: The boundary between the tertiary and quaternary sectors is blurred.

59340.q: Which activity belongs to the tertiary rather than the quaternary sector?
59340.e: Selling in retail is a classic service. Consulting, programming and research are knowledge-intensive and count as quaternary.
59340.m: Selling in a shop is a classic tertiary service.

59341.q: What characterises a hard location factor?
a: It can be measured and expressed in costs
It is based on personal preferences
59341.e: Hard location factors such as land prices, taxes or transport links can be recorded in figures and included directly in a company's cost calculations.
59341.m: Hard location factors can be measured.

59342.q: What is meant by competition between locations?
a: Firms compete for the same raw material
59342.e: Countries, cantons and municipalities try to attract firms and jobs with taxes, infrastructure and quality of life.
59342.m: In competition between locations, regions try to win companies.

59343.q: Which two kinds of soft location factors are often distinguished?
59343.e: Company-related soft factors concern, for example, the business climate. People-related ones concern employees' quality of life, such as culture and leisure facilities.
59343.m: Soft location factors concern either the company or the people.

59344.q: Which hard location factor is one reason why the canton of Zug attracts many company headquarters?
59344.e: Compared with the rest of Switzerland, Zug has low tax rates for companies. That is a measurable cost advantage.
59344.m: Low taxes are a hard location factor.

59345.q: Which location factor is becoming increasingly important for highly qualified specialists?
a: Location on a river as a source of energy
59345.e: Well-trained specialists can often choose where they work. That is why firms pay attention to attractive living conditions in order to attract staff.
59345.m: Quality of life is an important soft location factor.

a: Advantages of being close to other companies
Advantages from a large company car park
59346.e: Contact advantages arise when firms are close together and can easily exchange contacts, information and orders.
59346.m: Contact advantages come from being close to partners.

59347.q: What is a company called whose choice of location is mainly determined by being close to its customers?
59347.e: For market-oriented businesses, such as shops or bakeries, being close to the market is decisive.
59347.m: Market-oriented businesses locate close to their customers.

59348.q: Which location orientation was typical of early aluminium smelters, for example in Valais?
59348.e: Making aluminium needs a great deal of electricity. That is why smelters were built where cheap hydropower was available, as in Valais.
59348.m: Electricity-hungry businesses look for locations with cheap energy.

59349.q: Why has transport cost as a location factor become less important for many industries since the 20th century?
a: Transport became much cheaper and faster
There are fewer roads than before
59349.e: Container shipping, motorways and air freight greatly lowered the cost per tonne. Other factors such as workers or taxes became more important as a result.
59349.m: Cheap transport makes other location factors more important.

59350.q: Which of the following is a hard location factor?
59350.e: The number of available skilled workers and the wage level can be measured. Cultural offering, reputation and political climate are more soft factors.
59350.m: The availability of workers counts as a hard location factor.

59351.q: Who published the work “Theory of the Location of Industries” (Über den Standort der Industrien) in 1909?
59351.e: With it, the economist Alfred Weber, brother of the sociologist Max Weber, founded the classic theory of industrial location.
59351.m: Alfred Weber founded industrial location theory in 1909.

59352.q: According to Weber's theory, which location does a business look for first and foremost?
a: The place with the lowest transport costs
The place with the highest prices
The place with the most inhabitants
The place with the nicest climate
59352.e: Weber assumed that transport costs are the most important factor. The best location keeps the costs of transporting raw materials and finished products as low as possible.
59352.m: For Weber, what matters most is the lowest transport cost.

59353.q: How is Weber's material index calculated?
a: Weight of localised materials divided by the weight of the product
Weight of the product divided by the number of workers
Price of the product divided by the transport distance
Number of raw materials divided by the number of markets
59353.e: The material index compares how much weight of location-bound raw materials goes into a product. It shows whether the business tends towards the raw material or the market.
59353.m: The material index compares the weight of raw materials and the weight of the product.

59354.q: To make 1 tonne of product, 4 tonnes of localised raw materials are needed. What is the material index?
59354.e: The material index is 4 t divided by 1 t, so 4. A value above 1 points to a location near the raw material.
59354.m: A high material index pulls the business to the raw material site.

59355.q: According to Weber, where does a business tend to locate if the material index is less than 1?
a: Near where the raw material is found
59355.e: If the product is heavier than the localised raw materials, for example because ubiquitous materials are added, it pays to produce near the market.
59355.m: If the material index is less than 1, production takes place near the market.

59356.q: According to Weber, why does a raw material like water hardly influence a factory's choice of location?
a: It is never used in products
59356.e: Weber called raw materials available everywhere ubiquities. Because they can be got anywhere, they do not pull a business to any particular place. They do, however, add to the weight of the product.
59356.m: Raw materials available everywhere are called ubiquities.

59357.q: According to Weber's logic, why are breweries more likely to be near the market?
a: The heavy water is a ubiquity
Beer goes off immediately when transported
59357.e: Beer consists mostly of water, which is available everywhere. Transporting the finished, heavy product would be expensive, so it is produced near the customers.
59357.m: Breweries are market-oriented because water is available everywhere.

59358.q: According to Weber, when does a business move away from the point of lowest transport cost to cheaper workers?
a: When the wage saving is greater than the extra transport costs
When transport costs rise and wages stay the same
Always, as soon as wages are lower somewhere
Never, transport costs always come first
59358.e: For this, Weber drew isodapanes, lines of equal extra transport cost. If the wage saving at a place is greater than the extra transport cost, moving pays off.
59358.m: Changing location pays off when the saving exceeds the extra costs.

59359.q: Which geometric figure does Weber use to find the best location between two raw material sites and a market?
59359.e: In the location triangle, the two raw material sites and the market are at the corners. The best location is the point where total transport costs are lowest.
59359.m: Weber found the location using the location triangle.

59360.q: According to Weber, which two factors can draw a business away from the point of lowest transport cost?
a: Many public holidays and short working hours
59360.e: Weber added labour costs and agglomeration to transport costs. If the saving is worth more than the extra transport costs, the location shifts.
59360.m: Labour costs and agglomeration can shift the location.

59361.q: Who developed the model of von Thünen's rings?
59361.e: Johann Heinrich von Thünen was a landowner and economist in Mecklenburg. He presented his model of agricultural land use in the 19th century.
59361.m: Von Thünen's rings go back to Johann Heinrich von Thünen.

59362.q: What is the work called in which von Thünen presented his model in 1826?
a: Theory of the Location of Industries
59362.e: In the first volume of “The Isolated State” (1826), von Thünen developed his model of a city in a uniform plain without foreign trade.
59362.m: Von Thünen described his model in the work “The Isolated State”.

59363.q: In the von Thünen model, which quantity decreases with increasing distance from the city?
59363.e: As the distance grows, transport costs rise, so the profit per area, called the location rent, falls.
59363.m: Location rent falls with distance from the market.

59364.q: Which land use was in the innermost ring?
59364.e: Fresh products that go off quickly, such as vegetables and milk, had to get to market fast. That is why they were produced very close to the city.
59364.m: Perishable products were produced close to the city.

59365.q: Why did forestry lie in the second ring in von Thünen's model, fairly close to the city?
a: Wood was heavy and much needed in the city
Wood was the most expensive export
The forest protected the city from enemies
59365.e: Wood was used as fuel and building material and was very heavy compared with its value. Long journeys by horse and cart would not have paid off.
59365.m: Heavy goods such as wood were produced close to the market.

59366.q: Which land use lay in the outermost ring, before the untouched wilderness?
59366.e: Animals can walk to market themselves, and livestock farming needs a lot of land with a low yield per hectare. That is why it pays even far from the city.
59366.m: In the von Thünen model, livestock farming is the outermost land use.

59367.q: Yield 10 t/ha, market price 200 francs/t, production costs 120 francs/t, freight rate 2 francs per t and km. What is the location rent 20 km away?
59367.e: Location rent equals 10 times (200 minus 120) minus 10 times 2 times 20. That gives 800 minus 400, so 400 francs per hectare.
59367.m: Location rent is revenue minus production and transport costs.

59368.q: Yield 10 t/ha, price 200 francs/t, production costs 120 francs/t, freight rate 2 francs per t and km. At what distance does the location rent become zero?
59368.e: The profit without transport is 10 times 80, so 800 francs. Transport costs are 20 francs per km and hectare. 800 divided by 20 gives 40 km.
59368.m: Where the location rent is zero, growing a product stops.

59369.q: Which assumption is part of von Thünen's model of the isolated state?
a: A uniform plain with equally fertile soil everywhere
59369.e: Von Thünen simplified a great deal: a single city, an even plain without rivers or mountains, and no foreign trade. Only the distance to the market was supposed to determine land use.
59369.m: Von Thünen's model assumes a uniform plain.

59370.q: How does the shape of the rings change if a navigable river leads to the city?
a: They are stretched out along the river
They move to the other side of the city
59370.e: Transport costs are lower along the river. That is why intensive land use pays there even further from the city, and the zones stretch out along the river.
59370.m: A river distorts von Thünen's rings along its course.

59371.q: In which US state is Silicon Valley?
59371.e: Silicon Valley lies at the southern end of San Francisco Bay, mainly in the Santa Clara Valley.

59372.q: Where does the name “Silicon Valley” come from?
a: From silicon used for semiconductor chips
From silicone used in beauty products
59372.e: Silicon is the basic material for semiconductors and computer chips, which were developed there from the 1950s.
59372.m: Silicon Valley is named after the chip material silicon.

59373.q: Which university is seen as an important starting point for the rise of Silicon Valley?
59373.e: Stanford University in Palo Alto encouraged students to found companies early on and opened an industrial park on its land in 1951.
59373.m: Stanford University played a key role for Silicon Valley.

59374.q: What did Stanford University do in 1951 to bring technology firms close to it?
a: It opened an industrial park on its land
It banned students from founding companies
It bought a chip factory in Texas
59374.e: At the suggestion of Professor Frederick Terman, Stanford leased land to technology firms. This industrial park became a seed of Silicon Valley.
59374.m: An industrial park at Stanford University helped Silicon Valley grow.

59375.q: In economic geography, what does the term cluster describe?
a: A spatial concentration of linked firms and institutions
A firm with many branches abroad
An area with no industry at all
A state monopoly in one industry
59375.e: In a cluster, companies, suppliers, universities and investors in one industry work closely together in one place and benefit from each other.
59375.m: A cluster is a concentration of linked companies in one industry.

59376.q: Which economist made the cluster concept particularly well known in the 1990s?
59376.e: Michael E. Porter of Harvard Business School shaped the cluster concept in his book on the competitive advantage of nations (1990).
59376.m: Michael Porter made the cluster concept well known.

59377.q: Which form of financing is particularly typical of the many start-ups in Silicon Valley?
59377.e: Venture capitalists invest in young firms with high growth potential and take a high risk of failure in return.
59377.m: Start-ups in Silicon Valley are often financed with venture capital.

59378.q: What is meant by a spin-off?
a: A new company that grows out of a firm or university
A factory that is closed down
A customs agreement between two states
59378.e: Employees or researchers use their knowledge to found their own firm. Such spin-offs have made Silicon Valley grow strongly.
59378.m: A spin-off grows out of an existing firm or university.

59379.q: Which location advantage arises in Silicon Valley from the many specialists in a small area?
a: Fast exchange of knowledge and staff
59379.e: Specialists often change jobs and pass on knowledge. This exchange of knowledge is a typical agglomeration advantage.
59379.m: In a cluster, knowledge spreads especially fast.

59380.q: Which disadvantage is linked to the success of Silicon Valley?
a: Very high rents and a housing shortage
No transport routes to the sea
59380.e: Strong demand for housing from well-paid specialists has made rents and house prices rise sharply.
59380.m: Successful clusters often suffer from high housing costs.

59381.q: What does the term “Rust Belt” refer to?
a: A belt of rusting old industry
59381.e: The term refers to the rusty, closed factories and steelworks that make the decline of industry visible.
59381.m: The Rust Belt is named after rusting old factories.

a: In the north-east and Midwest of the USA
In the south-west of the USA
On the west coast of Canada
59382.e: The Rust Belt stretches roughly from Pennsylvania via Ohio and Indiana to Michigan and the Great Lakes.
59382.m: The Rust Belt lies in the north-east and Midwest of the USA.

59383.q: Which city is considered the centre of the US car industry in the Rust Belt?
59383.e: Detroit, the “Motor City”, was home to the big car companies and lost a large part of its population as the industry declined.
59383.m: Detroit is the best-known car city in the USA.

59384.q: Which city in the Rust Belt was known as “Steel City” and is now an example of successful structural change?
59384.e: After the collapse of the steel industry in the 1980s, Pittsburgh turned to universities, medicine and technology.
59384.m: Pittsburgh changed from a steel city into a city of knowledge.

59385.q: From which decade did the sharp decline of industry in the Rust Belt begin?
59385.e: In the 1970s and 1980s, hundreds of thousands of jobs were lost in the steel and car industries.
59385.m: The decline of the Rust Belt began in the 1970s.

59386.q: Which reason contributed greatly to the decline of the Rust Belt?
a: Strong competition from abroad, for example from Japan
59386.e: Foreign manufacturers produced more cheaply and with more modern methods. Automation and factories moving to other regions also played a part.
59386.m: Foreign competition weakened industry in the Rust Belt.

59387.q: What is the region in the south of the USA called to which many jobs and people moved from the Rust Belt?
59387.e: The Sun Belt, with states such as Texas, Florida or Arizona, attracted people with its warm climate, low wages and weaker trade unions.
59387.m: Many jobs moved from the Rust Belt to the Sun Belt.

59388.q: In which year did Detroit file for bankruptcy, the largest US city to do so up to then?
59388.e: In July 2013 Detroit applied for protection from its creditors. It was the largest municipal bankruptcy in US history.

59389.q: Which region in Germany is seen as a counterpart to the Rust Belt with similar structural change?
59389.e: In the Ruhr, coal and steel shaped the economy for a long time. After many mines and steelworks closed, the region, like the Rust Belt, had to build up new industries.
59389.m: The Ruhr is the German example of structural change in an old industrial region.

59390.q: Which transport of raw materials encouraged heavy industry to settle in the Rust Belt area?
a: Transport of ore and coal across the Great Lakes
Transport of oil across the Pacific
Transport of cotton through the Mississippi Delta
59390.e: Iron ore from the Lake Superior region and coal from the Appalachians could be brought together cheaply by ship and rail.
59390.m: Ore and coal made the region a centre of heavy industry.

59391.q: In which year were the first special economic zones of the People's Republic of China set up?
59391.e: In 1980 the first four zones were created as part of the reform and opening-up policy.
59391.m: The first Chinese special economic zones were created in 1980.

59392.q: Under which Chinese politician did the reform and opening-up policy, from which the special economic zones came, begin?
59392.e: From 1978, Deng Xiaoping introduced economic reforms that allowed market economy elements and foreign investment.
59392.m: Deng Xiaoping opened up China's economy from 1978.

59393.q: Which city opposite Hong Kong is the best-known Chinese special economic zone?
59393.e: Shenzhen borders directly on Hong Kong and developed from a small town into a metropolis of millions and a technology centre.
59393.m: Shenzhen is China's best-known special economic zone.

59394.q: Which group correctly names all four of China's first special economic zones from 1980?
59394.e: Three of the zones were in Guangdong Province, and Xiamen was in Fujian. All are on the south-east coast.
59394.m: The first zones were all on China's south-east coast.

59395.q: Which entire province was declared a special economic zone in 1988?
59395.e: In 1988 the island of Hainan became a province in its own right and at the same time a special economic zone as a whole.
59395.m: In 1988 Hainan became a special economic zone as an entire province.

59396.q: Why was Zhuhai chosen as a special economic zone?
a: Because it is close to Macau
Because it lies in high mountains
Because it is close to Mongolia
59396.e: Zhuhai borders Macau, which was then under Portuguese administration. Being close was meant to attract capital and know-how.
59396.m: Zhuhai benefits from being next to Macau.

59397.q: Which benefits did the special economic zones offer foreign investors?
a: Free raw materials from the state
Exemption from all labour laws worldwide
A separate currency for each firm
59397.e: Companies received lower tax rates, easier customs rules for importing parts and more freedom to run their business.
59397.m: Special economic zones attract investors with tax and customs advantages.

59398.q: What kind of investment were the special economic zones mainly meant to attract?
59398.e: Foreign firms were meant to build factories, bring capital and technology and create jobs.
59398.m: Special economic zones are meant to attract foreign direct investment.

59400.q: What role were the special economic zones meant to play for the rest of China?
a: They served as a testing ground for market economy reforms
They were meant to replace agriculture
They were planned as military bases
They were meant to prevent foreign trade
59400.e: The government tested new rules in the zones. What worked well was later extended to other regions.
59400.m: The special economic zones were laboratories for China's reforms.

59401.q: In which country are the maquiladoras?
59401.e: Maquiladoras are assembly plants in Mexico that mostly produce for the US market.

a: They assemble duty-free imported parts for export
They extract raw materials for the domestic market
They produce only food for Mexico
59402.e: The plants import components without duty, put them together with cheap labour and export the finished products again.
59402.m: Maquiladoras assemble imported parts for export.

59403.q: In which region of Mexico are particularly many maquiladoras located?
a: On the border with the USA
On the Pacific coast in the south
59403.e: Being close to the US market lowers transport costs and delivery times. Cities such as Tijuana or Ciudad Juárez became industrial centres as a result.
59403.m: Most maquiladoras are near the US border.

59404.q: What is the 1965 programme called with which Mexico started the maquiladora industry?
59404.e: After the end of the Bracero Program for farm workers in the USA, Mexico wanted to create jobs in the border area with this programme.
59404.m: The maquiladoras arose in 1965 with the Border Industrialization Program.

59405.q: Which location factor is particularly important for maquiladoras?
a: Low labour costs close to the US market
59405.e: Mexican wages are much lower than in the USA, and at the same time the market is only a few kilometres away.
59405.m: Maquiladoras combine low wages with being close to the market.

59406.q: What is the principle called in which imported parts are processed further abroad and exported again?
59406.e: In outward processing, mainly labour is added. The value added in the country therefore often stays low.

59407.q: Which 1994 free trade agreement boosted the growth of the maquiladoras?
59407.e: The North American Free Trade Agreement between the USA, Canada and Mexico removed customs duties and encouraged closer links in production.

59408.e: The United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement came into force on 1 July 2020 and includes, among other things, stricter rules of origin for cars.
59408.m: Since 2020, the USMCA has applied instead of NAFTA.

59409.q: Which industry is particularly strongly represented in the maquiladoras?
59409.e: Many maquiladoras assemble wiring harnesses, car parts, televisions or other electronics for the North American market.
59409.m: Maquiladoras often make electronics and car parts.

59410.q: Which criticism is often made of maquiladoras?
a: Low wages and difficult working conditions
Too much tax revenue for Mexico
Too few exports to the USA
59410.e: Critics point to low wages, long working hours, weak trade unions and environmental problems in the border area.
59410.m: Maquiladoras are criticised because of their working conditions.

59411.q: What is the aim of just-in-time production?
a: To deliver parts exactly when they are needed
To build up the largest possible stores
To produce only once a year
59411.e: Material should be at the production line at the right time and in the right amount. This greatly reduces stock levels and storage costs.
59411.m: Just in time means delivering on time without large stores.

59412.q: Which car manufacturer developed just-in-time production as part of its production system?
59412.e: The Toyota Production System arose in Japan from the 1950s and became a model for lean production worldwide.
59412.m: Just in time comes from the Toyota Production System.

59413.q: What did Toyota mainly want to achieve with just-in-time production in the post-war period?
a: To avoid waste from stockpiles and overproduction
To create as many jobs as possible
To build cars only for export
To build up large reserves for crises
59413.e: From the 1950s, the engineer Taiichi Ohno built up a system at Toyota that was meant to cut every kind of waste. Overproduction and full stores were seen as particularly costly.
59413.m: Just in time is meant to avoid waste.

59414.q: What is the card system called that is used to request new supplies in just in time?
59414.e: Kanban is Japanese for card or sign. When a container is empty, the card goes back to the previous station and triggers exactly the delivery needed.

59415.q: On which principle does just-in-time control work?
59415.e: In the pull principle, consumption pulls production along. Only what the following stages actually need is produced.
59415.m: Just in time works on the pull principle.

59416.q: What does the expression “the warehouse on the road” mean in connection with just in time?
a: Lorries take over the role of the warehouse
The factory stores parts on the pavement
Roads are rented out as car parks
59416.e: Because hardly any parts are stored in the factory any more, goods are constantly on the move. This increases lorry traffic.
59416.m: In just in time, traffic becomes a rolling warehouse.

59417.q: What is the further development called in which parts are delivered in the exact order of assembly?
59417.e: In just in sequence, car seats, for example, arrive in exactly the order in which the vehicles are on the production line.
59417.m: Just in sequence delivers parts in the order of assembly.

59418.q: What spatial consequence does just in time often have for suppliers?
a: They locate close to the assembly plant
They move to countries as far away as possible
They move their plants to the sea
59418.e: Short distances make on-time deliveries more reliable. That is why supplier parks grow up near large car plants.
59418.m: Just in time draws suppliers close to the plants.

59419.q: Which risk is linked to just-in-time production?
a: Interrupted deliveries can quickly stop production
59419.e: Without safety stocks, material runs out immediately in the event of strikes, accidents or border closures. This was seen, for example, in the chip shortage from 2021.
59419.m: Without stores, a small disruption can stop all production.

59420.q: Which event in March 2021 blocked an important sea trade route for days and showed how vulnerable global supply chains are?
a: The blocking of the Suez Canal by the “Ever Given”
The closure of the Panama Canal by an earthquake
The closure of the Gotthard road tunnel
A strike in the port of Rotterdam
59420.e: The container ship “Ever Given” ran aground in the Suez Canal and blocked it for about six days. Hundreds of ships were held up.
59420.m: The blocking of the Suez Canal in 2021 showed how vulnerable supply chains are.

a: It has subsidiaries in several countries
It sells only in its own country
It is owned jointly by several states
It is a sub-organisation of the UN
59421.e: Transnational or multinational companies produce and sell through subsidiaries in several countries. The management usually stays in one home country.
59421.m: A transnational company operates with its own sites in many countries.

59422.q: In which town in the canton of Vaud does the food company Nestlé have its headquarters?
59422.e: Nestlé has its headquarters in Vevey on Lake Geneva. The company is one of the largest food companies in the world.

59423.q: The merger of which two Basel firms created the pharmaceutical company Novartis in 1996?
59423.e: Novartis was created in 1996 from the merger of Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz and has its headquarters in Basel. The company operates with subsidiaries in many countries.
59423.m: Novartis was created in 1996 from Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz.

59424.q: What are the prices called that subsidiaries of the same company charge each other for goods and services?
59424.e: Transfer prices apply to business within a group of companies. They can be used to shift profits between countries, which is why tax authorities check them closely.
59424.m: Business within a group of companies is charged at transfer prices.

59425.q: What is a foreign direct investment?
a: A stake with lasting influence on a foreign firm
A short-term purchase of shares for speculation
A donation to an aid organisation abroad
A loan from one state to another country
59425.e: In a direct investment, a company builds or buys a firm abroad or takes such a large stake that it has a say. Pure financial investments without influence are called portfolio investments.
59425.m: Direct investments give influence over a company abroad.

59426.q: What is a company called whose main purpose is to hold stakes in other firms over the long term?
59426.e: A holding company usually produces nothing itself but holds and steers stakes. Many international groups are organised as a holding company with many subsidiaries.
59426.m: A holding company holds and steers stakes in other companies.

59427.q: What is the minimum tax rate under the OECD/G20 minimum taxation for large international companies?
59427.e: The global minimum tax applies to groups with a turnover of at least 750 million euros. Switzerland has applied it since 2024 with a top-up tax, after the people approved it in 2023.
59427.m: Large companies are meant to pay at least 15 percent tax on profits worldwide.

59428.q: Why did the Responsible Business Initiative fail in November 2020, even though just over half of voters said yes?
a: It did not win a majority of the cantons
59428.e: A popular initiative needs a majority of the people and of the cantons. The initiative received about 50.7 percent yes votes, but most cantons rejected it.
59428.m: A popular initiative needs both a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons.

59429.q: What are the OECD's recommendations for companies operating globally called, for which every participating country runs a National Contact Point?
59429.e: The OECD Guidelines cover, for example, human rights, working conditions and the environment. In Switzerland the National Contact Point is at SECO, where complaints against companies can be made.
59429.m: The OECD Guidelines give multinational companies rules for responsible behaviour.

59430.q: In which steps of a smartphone's value chain is most money usually made?
59430.e: If you plot the value added along the chain, you get a smiling shape, the smile curve. A lot is earned at the beginning and the end, and little in assembly.
59430.m: The most money is earned at the beginning and end of the chain.

59431.q: Which metal from the ore coltan is used in smartphones for tiny capacitors?
59431.e: Coltan contains the metals tantalum and niobium. Tantalum capacitors are very small and powerful and are therefore common in mobile phones.
59431.m: Tantalum for capacitors is obtained from coltan.

59432.q: What are firms like Foxconn called that assemble electronics on behalf of other brands?
59432.e: Contract manufacturers (electronic manufacturing services) produce devices that are sold under the names of other brands. Foxconn from Taiwan assembles many smartphones in China in this way.
59432.m: A contract manufacturer produces devices for other brands.

59433.q: Which company from Taiwan is the world's largest contract manufacturer of semiconductor chips?
59433.e: TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company) makes chips to the designs of other firms. It has the largest market share in the foundry business.
59433.m: TSMC in Taiwan is the world's largest contract chip manufacturer.

59434.q: In which country has the mining of conflict minerals such as coltan financed armed groups for years?
59434.e: In the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, militias control many mines. The EU therefore requires due diligence when tin, tantalum, tungsten and gold are imported.
59434.m: Conflict minerals finance armed groups, especially in the Congo.

59435.q: In which country is Agbogbloshie, which became known as a hub for electronic waste?
59435.e: Agbogbloshie is an area in Accra, the capital of Ghana. Old electrical devices were often taken apart and burned there under dangerous conditions.
59435.m: Agbogbloshie in Accra stands for the problems with electronic waste.

59436.q: Which US businessman is considered the inventor of modern container transport?
59436.e: In 1956 the haulier Malcom McLean had containers transported for the first time on the converted tanker “Ideal X”. This lowered handling costs massively.
59436.m: Malcom McLean made the container the standard in shipping.

59437.q: Measured by container throughput, which was the largest port in Europe in 2024?
59437.e: In 2024 Rotterdam handled about 13.8 million TEU, just ahead of Antwerp-Bruges with about 13.5 million TEU. Worldwide, however, the largest container ports are in Asia.
59437.m: Rotterdam is Europe's largest container port.

59438.q: In which Swiss city does MSC, the world's largest container shipping company (as of 2025), have its headquarters?
59438.e: The Mediterranean Shipping Company was founded in 1970 and is based in Geneva. In 2022 it overtook the Danish company Maersk as the largest container shipping company.
59438.m: The world's largest container shipping company is based in landlocked Switzerland, in Geneva.

59439.q: What is it called when container ships deliberately sail more slowly to save fuel?
59439.e: Fuel consumption rises disproportionately with speed. Shipping companies therefore often lower their speed and so save costs and CO2.
59439.m: Sailing more slowly saves ships a lot of fuel.

59440.q: What is the flag of a country such as Panama or Liberia called, under which shipping companies register ships because of low costs?
59440.e: With a flag of convenience, a ship is registered in a country with which the owner has little to do. The reasons are low fees, taxes and less strict rules.
59440.m: Ships sail under flags of convenience because of lower costs.

59441.q: Where is the transfer point through which container ships on the Rhine reach Switzerland?
59441.e: The Swiss Rhine Ports are in and around Basel. Rhine ships connect them with the seaports of Rotterdam and Antwerp.
59441.m: Switzerland is connected to the sea via the Rhine ports of Basel.

59442.q: Why is the Strait of Malacca near Singapore considered one of the most sensitive bottlenecks in world shipping?
a: The shipping lane there is only a few kilometres wide
Icebergs drift there all year round
59442.e: In the Phillips Channel near Singapore, the shipping lane is only just under three kilometres wide. Hundreds of large ships crowd through there every day.
59442.m: Near Singapore, the shipping route is only just under three kilometres wide.

59443.q: What is China's worry called that a large part of its oil imports has to pass through the Strait of Malacca?
59443.e: The term became known in 2003 under President Hu Jintao. A blockade of the strait could badly hit China's energy supply.
59443.m: The Malacca dilemma describes China's dependence on a single strait.

59444.q: Which security problem particularly affected the Strait of Malacca at the beginning of the 2000s?
59444.e: At the beginning of the 2000s, many attacks on ships were reported there. Joint patrols by Malaysia, Indonesia and Singapore greatly reduced the number.
59444.m: Joint patrols pushed back piracy in the Strait of Malacca.

59445.q: What does the term “Malaccamax” mean in shipping?
a: The largest ships that can still pass through the Strait of Malacca
The highest water level in the Strait of Malacca
The maximum speed allowed in the strait
The largest port facility in the city of Malacca
59445.e: The main limit is the shallow water near Singapore. Malaccamax ships have a draught of at most about 20 metres; even larger tankers have to use other straits.
59445.m: Malaccamax means the maximum ship size for the Strait of Malacca.

59446.q: Which strait in Indonesia do very large tankers use as an alternative route if their draught is too deep for Malacca?
59446.e: The Lombok Strait between Bali and Lombok is much deeper than the Strait of Malacca. But the detour takes extra time.
59446.m: Ships with a very deep draught switch to the Lombok Strait.

59447.q: Through which country would the long-discussed Kra Canal run, which would bypass the Strait of Malacca?
59447.e: The Kra Isthmus is the narrowest point of the Malay Peninsula, in southern Thailand. A canal there would shorten the sea route by several hundred kilometres, but it has never been built.
59447.m: The planned Kra Canal would run through Thailand.

59448.q: Which event triggered the Suez Crisis in 1956?
a: The canal collapsed in an earthquake
59448.e: In July 1956 President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal Company. Great Britain, France and Israel then intervened militarily, but had to withdraw.
59448.m: Nasser's nationalisation of the canal led to the Suez Crisis in 1956.

59449.q: From when to when was the Suez Canal closed after the Six-Day War?
59449.e: After the Six-Day War in 1967, the canal formed the front line between Egypt and Israel. It was only reopened to shipping in 1975.
59449.m: The Suez Canal was closed for eight years, from 1967 to 1975.

59450.q: Roughly how long is the Suez Canal?
59450.e: The canal is about 193 kilometres long. This makes it one of the longest artificial waterways in the world.
59450.m: The Suez Canal is just under 200 kilometres long.

59451.q: Around which cape did many shipping companies divert from the end of 2023, when attacks in the Red Sea made the Suez route unsafe?
59451.e: Because of attacks by the Houthi militia on merchant ships, many shipping companies sailed around the southern tip of Africa. As a result, the journey to Europe often took ten to fourteen days longer.
59451.m: Without the Suez Canal, the route from Asia to Europe goes around the Cape of Good Hope.

59452.q: Since when has the World Trade Organization (WTO) existed?
59452.e: The WTO was created on 1 January 1995 as a result of the Uruguay Round. It took over and extended the rules of the earlier General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.

59453.q: What is the WTO round of negotiations called that started in Qatar in 2001 and has still not been completed?
59453.e: The Doha Round was meant above all to bring benefits to developing countries. Disputes over farm subsidies and market access prevented an agreement.
59453.m: The WTO's Doha Round began in 2001 and was never completed.

59454.q: Which Nigerian economist has been Director-General of the WTO since 2021 (as of 2026)?
59454.e: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala was previously Nigeria's finance minister. She is the first woman and the first person from Africa to head the WTO and was confirmed for a second term in 2024.
59454.m: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala has led the WTO since 2021.

59455.q: How many members does the WTO have (as of 2025)?
59455.e: With the Comoros and Timor-Leste joining in 2024, the number rose to 166 members. They account for most of world trade.
59455.m: Almost all countries in the world are members of the WTO.

59456.q: What is the WTO principle called according to which a trade advantage for one country must be granted to all members?
59456.e: Under the most-favoured-nation principle, a WTO member may not treat any other member worse than its best trading partner. There are exceptions, for example for free trade agreements.
59456.m: Most-favoured-nation treatment means the same advantages for all WTO members.

59457.q: Which WTO principle requires that imported goods are not treated worse than local ones once they have cleared customs?
59457.e: National treatment forbids, for example, higher taxes or stricter rules only for foreign products. It applies as soon as a product has entered the market.
59457.m: Imported goods may not be put at a disadvantage in the domestic market.

59458.q: Why has the WTO dispute settlement Appellate Body been blocked since the end of 2019?
a: The USA is preventing new judges from being appointed
Switzerland has cancelled the headquarters agreement
The EU no longer pays contributions
59458.e: The Appellate Body needs at least three judges. Because the USA is blocking new appointments, it has not been able to make decisions since December 2019.
59458.m: Without new judges, the WTO Appellate Body cannot make decisions.

59459.q: In which year did China join the WTO?
59459.e: China became a member of the WTO in December 2001. After that, its exports rose very sharply.
59459.m: China has been a member of the WTO since 2001.

59460.q: What does the WTO's TRIPS agreement regulate?
a: The protection of patents, trademarks and copyright
The level of customs duties on cars
59460.e: The TRIPS agreement sets minimum standards for patents, copyright and trademark rights. Trade in services, on the other hand, is regulated by GATS.
59460.m: In the WTO, TRIPS protects intellectual property.

59461.q: What distinguishes a free trade area from a customs union?
a: Each country keeps its own customs duties towards third countries
The borders are open to people
There is a common external tariff
59461.e: In a free trade area, only the customs duties between the partners are removed. A customs union such as the EU also has a common external tariff.
59461.m: Unlike a customs union, a free trade area has no common external tariff.

59462.q: Why are rules of origin needed in free trade agreements?
a: So that only goods from the partner countries are duty-free
So that goods are transported faster
So that all products cost the same
So that customs duties rise every year
59462.e: Rules of origin set how much of a product must be made in the partner country. This prevents third countries from routing goods through the country with the lowest duty.
59462.m: Rules of origin decide which goods count as goods from a partner country.

59463.q: In which year did Switzerland and the then EEC sign their free trade agreement for industrial goods?
59463.e: The 1972 free trade agreement removed customs duties on industrial goods. It is still a basis of trade between Switzerland and the EU today.
59463.m: Since 1972, a free trade agreement for industrial goods has applied between Switzerland and the EU.

59464.q: Which four countries are members of EFTA?
a: Switzerland, Great Britain, Iceland and Ireland
59464.e: The European Free Trade Association was founded in 1960. Today its members are Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein.
59464.m: EFTA consists of Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein.

59465.q: Which free trade agreement did Switzerland vote on in March 2021 and narrowly approve?
59465.e: A referendum had been called against the agreement with Indonesia, mainly because of palm oil. It was approved with about 51.6 percent yes votes.
